mcqs.why: (1, -2) has x positive and y negative — this is the fourth quadrant, not the first.

mcqs.q: The Cartesian plane is also called:
mcqs.why: The Cartesian plane formed by the x and y axes is also known as the xy-plane.

mcqs.q: In the second quadrant:
mcqs.why: Quadrant II is the upper-left region where x values are negative and y values are positive.

mcqs.q: Joining O(0,0), A(5,0), B(5,5), C(0,5) in order forms a:
mcqs.why: All four sides are 5 units and all angles are 90 degrees, so the figure is a square.

mcqs.why: y = 2 - x, so at x = 3, y = 2 - 3 = -1, matching the table in the source.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.2 — Drawing the Graph of a Straight Line
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

The graph of a first-degree equation in x and y is always a straight line. To draw it: make a table with at least two or three pairs (x, y) satisfying the equation, plot the points on graph paper with a suitable scale, and join them with a straight line using a ruler, extending it both ways.

Special lines: y = a number is a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis; x = a number is a vertical line parallel to the y-axis; y = 0 is the x-axis itself. A line through the origin, like y = 2x, passes through (0, 0).

Missing coordinates are found by substituting the known coordinate into the equation and solving for the other.

Formulas

y = k is parallel to the x-axis

x = k is parallel to the y-axis

Distance = Speed x Time

Example: Drawing y = 2x + 3

Draw the graph of y = 2x + 3.

Step 1: Choose x values 0, 1 and -1.

Step 2: Calculate y: at x = 0, y = 3; at x = 1, y = 5; at x = -1, y = 1.

Step 3: Plot the points (0, 3), (1, 5) and (-1, 1) on the axes.

Step 4: Join the plotted points with a straight ruler line and extend it both ways. The line cuts the y-axis at (0, 3).

Example: Horizontal and vertical lines

Describe the graphs of y = 3 and x = 3.

Step 1: For y = 3, every point has y-coordinate 3, whatever x is.

Step 2: Plot points like (0, 3), (2, 3), (-2, 3) and join them: a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis cutting the y-axis at (0, 3).

Step 3: For x = 3, every point has x-coordinate 3.

Step 4: Plot (3, 0), (3, 2), (3, -2) and join them: a vertical line parallel to the y-axis cutting the x-axis at (3, 0).

Example: Finding a missing coordinate

For 2x + y = 6, find y when x = 1 and find x when y = 0.

Step 1: Substitute x = 1: 2 + y = 6.

Step 2: Solve: y = 4, giving the point (1, 4).

Step 3: Substitute y = 0: 2x = 6.

Step 4: Solve: x = 3, giving the point (3, 0). Plotting both points and joining gives the line.

Example: Distance-time graph

Ayesha drives at 20 km per hour. Draw the distance-time graph and read off the time for 100 km and the distance in 3 hours.

Step 1: Use Distance = 20 x Time and make a table: time 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 hours gives distance 0, 20, 40, 60, 100 km.

Step 2: Plot time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis.

Step 3: Join the points: a straight line through the origin with slope 20.

Step 4: From the graph, 100 km needs 100/20 = 5 hours, and in 3 hours the distance is 20 x 3 = 60 km.

mcqs.q: The graph of y = 3 is:
options: A horizontal line parallel to the x-axis
A line through the origin only
mcqs.why: y = 3 keeps y constant, so all points lie on a horizontal line parallel to the x-axis through (0, 3).

mcqs.why: x = 5 keeps x constant, giving a vertical line, and vertical lines are parallel to the y-axis.

mcqs.why: y = (1/2)(4) = 2, so the point satisfying the equation is (4, 2).

mcqs.q: The graph of y = 0 is:
mcqs.why: y = 0 is satisfied by every point on the x-axis, so its graph is the x-axis itself.

mcqs.q: For 2x + 4y = 8, when x = 0 the point is:
mcqs.why: Substituting x = 0 gives 4y = 8, so y = 2 and the point is (0, 2).

mcqs.q: For x + y = 6, the pair in the table when x = 4 is:
mcqs.why: y = 6 - x = 6 - 4 = 2, so the pair is (4, 2) in the table for x + y = 6.

mcqs.q: Ayesha drives at 20 km/h. The time to travel 100 km is:
mcqs.why: Time = Distance / Speed = 100 / 20 = 5 hours, read from the distance-time graph.

mcqs.q: The line y = 2x + 3 passes through:
mcqs.why: At x = 0, y = 3, so (0, 3) is on the line; the line also passes through (1, 5) and (-1, 1).

mcqs.q: For the age-weight equation y = 2x, at age x = 5 the weight y is:
mcqs.why: y = 2x = 2 x 5 = 10, matching the age-weight table where the graph is a line through the origin.

mcqs.q: For x - y = 2, when y = 0 the missing coordinate gives the point:
mcqs.why: With y = 0, x - 0 = 2 gives x = 2, so the point is (2, 0).

lessons.title: Exercise 7.3 — Conversion Graphs and Graphical Solution of Simultaneous Equations
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

A conversion graph is a straight line graph between two units (for example miles and kilometres). To convert, find the given value on one axis, move straight to the line, then move across to the other axis and read the converted value. Conversion lines between proportional units pass through the origin.

Useful rates from this unit: 1 mile is about 1.6 km; 1 hectare is about 2.471 acres; 1 Saudi riyal is about 30 Pakistani rupees.

Temperature conversion uses a formula and its graph: Fahrenheit and centigrade are linked by F = (9/5)C + 32.

To solve two simultaneous linear equations graphically, draw both lines on the same axes. Their point of intersection gives the solution (x, y), which should be checked in both original equations. Parallel lines never meet, so there is no solution (empty set), for example x = 2 and x = 5.

Formulas

F = (9/5)C + 32

C = (5/9)(F - 32)

1 mile = 1.6 km (approximately)

Example: Miles and kilometres

Use the conversion graph to convert 3 miles into kilometres and 8 kilometres into miles.

Step 1: For 3 miles, go up from 3 on the miles axis to the conversion line, then across to the kilometres axis.

Step 2: Read the value: 3 miles = 4.8 km (3 x 1.6).

Step 3: For 8 km, go from 8 on the kilometres axis to the line, then across to the miles axis.

Step 4: Read the value: 8 km = 5 miles.

Example: Temperature conversion

Convert 80 degrees centigrade into Fahrenheit.

Step 1: Write the formula.

F = (9/5)C + 32

Step 2: Substitute C = 80.

F = (9/5)(80) + 32 = 144 + 32

Step 3: Simplify.

F = 176, so 80 C = 176 F

Example: Graphical solution of simultaneous equations

Solve graphically: y = 3x - 5 and x + y = 11.

Step 1: Make a table for the first line: points (0, -5), (2, 1), (4, 7); plot them and draw the line.

Step 2: Make a table for the second line, x + y = 11: points (0, 11), (4, 7), (11, 0); plot them and draw the line on the same axes.

Step 3: The two lines cross at the single point (4, 7); describe it as the intersection on the graph.

Step 4: Check: 7 = 3(4) - 5 = 7 and 4 + 7 = 11, both correct.

Solution: x = 4, y = 7

Example: Rupees and riyals

Convert 5.2 Saudi riyals into rupees using the graph rate 1 riyal = 30 rupees.

Step 1: Find 5.2 on the riyals axis and move to the conversion line.

Step 2: Move across and read the rupees value.

Step 3: Confirm by multiplication: 5.2 x 30 = 156.

5.2 riyals = 156 rupees

mcqs.why: The miles-kilometres conversion line gives 1 mile = 1.6 km approximately.

mcqs.q: 3 miles converted to kilometres is approximately:
mcqs.why: Multiply by the rate: 3 x 1.6 = 4.8, so 3 miles is approximately 4.8 km.

32 degrees Fahrenheit in centigrade is:

mcqs.why: 3 x 30 = 90, so 3 Saudi riyals convert to 90 Pakistani rupees on the graph.

mcqs.why: The lines intersect at (1, 1); check: 2(1)+1 = 3 and 1-1 = 0, both satisfied.

mcqs.why: Intersection is (4, 7): 7 = 3(4)-5 and 4+7 = 11, so both equations hold at (4, 7).

mcqs.why: Both are vertical lines; they are parallel and never meet, so the solution set is empty.

mcqs.why: 2 x 2.471 = 4.94 acres, which is approximately 5 acres as read from the graph.

mcqs.why: Divide by the rate: 150 / 30 = 5, so 150 rupees equal 5 Saudi riyals.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.1 — Solving by Factorization and Completing the Square
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

A quadratic equation is a polynomial equation in which the degree of the variable is 2. Its standard form is:

ax^2 + bx + c = 0, a != 0

A quadratic equation has at most 2 roots. A root is a value of x that satisfies the equation. Two main methods in this lesson are factorization and completing the square.

Method 1: Factorization

Step 1: Write the equation in standard form with zero on one side.

Step 2: Factorize the quadratic expression into two first-degree factors.

Step 3: Put each factor equal to zero, because if a product is zero then at least one factor is zero.

Step 4: Solve each linear equation to get the roots.

Example: Solve by factorization

x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0

Step 1: Find two numbers whose product is 6 and whose sum is 5. The numbers are 2 and 3.

Step 2: Factorize: (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0.

Step 3: Put each factor equal to zero: x + 2 = 0 or x + 3 = 0.

Step 4: Solve: x = -2 or x = -3.

Example: Solve by factorization with coefficients

6x^2 - x - 1 = 0

Step 1: Factorize the left side: (3x + 1)(2x - 1) = 0.

Step 2: Put each factor equal to zero: 3x + 1 = 0 or 2x - 1 = 0.

Step 3: Solve the first equation: 3x = -1, so x = -1/3.

Step 4: Solve the second equation: 2x = 1, so x = 1/2.

Method 2: Completing the Square

Step 1: Make the coefficient of x^2 equal to 1 by dividing if needed, and move the constant term to the right side.

Step 2: Add the square of half the coefficient of x to both sides.

Step 3: Write the left side as a perfect square.

Step 4: Take the square root of both sides, remembering both the positive and the negative root, and solve for x.

Example: Completing the square

x^2 + 6x + 1 = 0

Step 1: Move the constant: x^2 + 6x = -1.

Step 2: Half of 6 is 3, and 3^2 = 9. Add 9 to both sides: x^2 + 6x + 9 = 8.

Step 3: Write as a square: (x + 3)^2 = 8.

Step 4: Take square roots: x + 3 = +/- 2sqrt(2).

Step 5: Solve: x = -3 +/- 2sqrt(2).

Example: Completing the square after dividing

2x^2 + 4x - 1 = 0

Step 1: Divide by 2 and rearrange: x^2 + 2x = 1/2.

Step 2: Half of 2 is 1, and 1^2 = 1. Add 1 to both sides: (x + 1)^2 = 3/2.

Step 3: Take square roots: x + 1 = +/- sqrt(3/2) = +/- sqrt(6)/2.

Step 4: Solve: x = -1 +/- sqrt(6)/2.

Example: Finding an unknown coefficient from a root

In the equation 3x^2 + bx - 8 = 0, x = 2 is one root. Find b and the other root.

Step 1: Put x = 2 in the equation: 3(4) + 2b - 8 = 0.

Step 2: Simplify: 4 + 2b = 0, so 2b = -4 and b = -2.

Step 3: The equation becomes 3x^2 - 2x - 8 = (3x + 4)(x - 2) = 0.

Step 4: Apart from x = 2, the other factor gives 3x + 4 = 0, so the other root is x = -4/3.

Remember: not every quadratic equation can be solved by factorization over the rational numbers, but completing the square and the quadratic formula always work.

mcqs.q: What is the degree of a quadratic equation?
mcqs.why: A quadratic equation is defined as a polynomial equation in which the highest power, that is the degree of the variable, is 2.

mcqs.q: What is the standard form of a quadratic equation?
mcqs.why: The standard form given in the Review Exercise is ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a != 0, because if a were 0 the equation would no longer be quadratic.

mcqs.q: What are the roots of x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0?
mcqs.why: Factorizing gives (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0, so x + 2 = 0 or x + 3 = 0, which gives x = -2 or x = -3.

mcqs.q: What are the roots of x^2 - 11x + 30 = 0?
mcqs.why: Factorizing gives (x - 5)(x - 6) = 0, so x - 5 = 0 gives x = 5 and x - 6 = 0 gives x = 6.

mcqs.q: What are the roots of 6x^2 - x - 1 = 0?
mcqs.why: Factorizing gives (3x + 1)(2x - 1) = 0, so 3x + 1 = 0 gives x = -1/3 and 2x - 1 = 0 gives x = 1/2.

mcqs.q: What are the roots of x^2 - 2x = 0?
mcqs.why: Taking x common gives x(x - 2) = 0, so either x = 0 or x - 2 = 0, which gives the second root x = 2.

mcqs.q: Solving (x - 5)^2 - 9 = 0 gives which roots?
mcqs.why: First (x - 5)^2 = 9, so x - 5 = +/-3. Then x = 5 + 3 = 8 or x = 5 - 3 = 2, giving roots 8 and 2.

mcqs.q: By completing the square, x^2 + 6x + 1 = 0 gives which solution?
mcqs.why: Adding 9 to both sides gives (x + 3)^2 = 8, so x + 3 = +/- sqrt(8) = +/- 2sqrt(2), hence x = -3 +/- 2sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: In 3x^2 + bx - 8 = 0, if x = 2 is a root, what is b?
mcqs.why: Substituting x = 2 gives 3(4) + 2b - 8 = 0, so 4 + 2b = 0, which gives 2b = -4 and therefore b = -2.

mcqs.q: What is the maximum number of roots of a quadratic equation?
mcqs.why: A quadratic equation has degree 2, so it has at most 2 roots, as stated in the Review Exercise, counting a double root as a repeated root.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.2 — Solving by the Quadratic Formula
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

Every quadratic equation in standard form can be solved by the quadratic formula. First write the equation as:

ax^2 + bx + c = 0, a != 0

Formulas

x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a)

The expression under the square root is called the discriminant:

D = b^2 - 4ac

If D is positive, there are two distinct real roots. If D = 0, there is a double (repeated) root. If D is negative, the roots are complex numbers involving i, where i^2 = -1.

Example: Using the formula with a perfect-square discriminant

x^2 - 2x = 15

Step 1: Write in standard form: x^2 - 2x - 15 = 0, so a = 1, b = -2, c = -15.

Step 2: Find the discriminant: D = 4 + 60 = 64.

Step 3: Apply the formula: x = (2 +/- 8) / 2.

Step 4: Solve both cases: x = (2 + 8)/2 = 5 or x = (2 - 8)/2 = -3.

Example: Using the formula

10x^2 + 19x - 15 = 0

Step 1: Here a = 10, b = 19, c = -15.

Step 2: Find the discriminant: D = 361 + 600 = 961 = 31^2.

Step 3: Apply the formula: x = (-19 +/- 31) / 20.

Step 4: Solve both cases: x = 12/20 = 3/5 or x = -50/20 = -5/2.

Example: Irrational roots

x^2 = -x + 1

Step 1: Write in standard form: x^2 + x - 1 = 0, so a = 1, b = 1, c = -1.

Step 2: Find the discriminant: D = 1 + 4 = 5.

Step 3: Apply the formula: x = (-1 +/- sqrt(5)) / 2.

Step 4: Since sqrt(5) cannot be simplified, the roots are x = (-1 + sqrt(5))/2 and x = (-1 - sqrt(5))/2.

Example: Complex roots

9x^2 = 12x - 49

Step 1: Write in standard form: 9x^2 - 12x + 49 = 0.

Step 2: Find the discriminant: D = 144 - 1764 = -1620, which is negative.

Step 3: Apply the formula: x = (12 +/- 18i sqrt(5)) / 18.

Step 4: Simplify by dividing by 6: x = (2 +/- 3i sqrt(5)) / 3. The roots are complex, not real.

Special Cases

For x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0, factorization gives (x - 3)^2 = 0, so x = 3 is a double root. For x^2 - 1 = 0, x^2 = 1, so x = +/-1.

mcqs.q: What is the quadratic formula for ax^2 + bx + c = 0?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise confirms the formula is x = (-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / (2a), with -b in the numerator, minus 4ac inside the root, and 2a in the denominator.

mcqs.q: For x^2 - 2x - 15 = 0, what is the discriminant?
mcqs.why: Here a = 1, b = -2, c = -15, so D = b^2 - 4ac = 4 - 4(1)(-15) = 4 + 60 = 64, a perfect square.

mcqs.q: What are the roots of x^2 - 2x = 15?
mcqs.why: Writing x^2 - 2x - 15 = 0 and using D = 64 gives x = (2 +/- 8)/2, so x = 5 or x = -3.

mcqs.q: For 10x^2 + 19x - 15 = 0, the discriminant 961 equals which square?
mcqs.why: D = 19^2 - 4(10)(-15) = 361 + 600 = 961, and the source shows 961 = 31^2, so sqrt(D) = 31 in the formula.

mcqs.q: What are the roots of x^2 + x - 1 = 0?
mcqs.why: With a = 1, b = 1, c = -1, D = 1 + 4 = 5, so the formula gives x = (-1 +/- sqrt(5)) / 2, which are irrational roots.

mcqs.q: What are the roots of 3x^2 - 2x + 2 = 0?
mcqs.why: Here D = 4 - 24 = -20, which is negative, so x = (2 +/- 2i sqrt(5))/6 = (1 +/- i sqrt(5))/3, a pair of complex roots.

mcqs.q: What is the root of x^2 - 6x + 9 = 0?
mcqs.why: Factorizing gives (x - 3)^2 = 0, so x - 3 = 0 twice, which means x = 3 is a double, or repeated, root.

mcqs.q: What is the solution set of 4x^2 - 16 = 0?
mcqs.why: Dividing gives x^2 = 4, so x = +/-2. The Review Exercise confirms the solution set is {+/-2}, not {+/-4}.

mcqs.q: What are the roots of 4x^2 - 10x = 0 by the formula?
mcqs.why: Here D = 100, so x = (10 +/- 10)/8. This gives x = 20/8 = 5/2 or x = 0/8 = 0, so the roots are 5/2 and 0.

mcqs.q: What are the first-degree factors of x^2 - 15x + 56?
mcqs.why: We need two numbers with product 56 and sum -15, namely -7 and -8, so x^2 - 15x + 56 = (x - 7)(x - 8), as in the Review Exercise.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.3 — Equations Reducible to Quadratic Equations
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

Some equations are not quadratic at first sight, but a suitable substitution turns them into a quadratic equation. Such equations are called equations reducible to quadratic equations.

Step 1: Choose a substitution, for example t = x^2, t = 2^x, or t equal to a repeated fraction or bracket.

Step 2: Rewrite the whole equation in terms of t so it becomes a quadratic in t.

Step 3: Solve the quadratic for t by factorization or the formula.

Step 4: Put back the original expression for t and solve for x. Never stop at the values of t.

Example: A biquadratic equation

x^4 - 8x^2 - 9 = 0

Step 1: Put x^2 = t. The equation becomes t^2 - 8t - 9 = 0.

Step 2: Factorize: (t - 9)(t + 1) = 0, so t = 9 or t = -1.

Step 3: If t = 9, then x^2 = 9, so x = +/-3.

Step 4: If t = -1, then x^2 = -1, so x = +/- i. The full solution is x = +/-3 or x = +/- i.

Example: A repeated fraction

(2x + 3)/(x + 1) + 6((x + 1)/(2x + 3)) = 7

Step 1: Put t = (2x + 3)/(x + 1). Note the second fraction is 1/t, so the equation becomes t + 6/t = 7.

Step 2: Multiply by t: t^2 - 7t + 6 = 0, which factorizes as (t - 1)(t - 6) = 0, so t = 1 or t = 6.

Step 3: If t = 1, then (2x + 3)/(x + 1) = 1, so 2x + 3 = x + 1 and x = -2.

Step 4: If t = 6, then (2x + 3)/(x + 1) = 6, so 2x + 3 = 6x + 6 and x = -3/4.

Example: An exponential equation

2^x + 16/2^x = 8

An equation involving powers like 2^x is called an exponential equation. The solution of 3^x = 9, for comparison, is x = 2 because 9 = 3^2.

Step 1: Put t = 2^x. The equation becomes t + 16/t = 8.

Step 2: Multiply by t: t^2 - 8t + 16 = 0, which is (t - 4)^2 = 0, so t = 4.

Step 3: Put back: 2^x = 4 = 2^2, so x = 2.

Example: A product of four factors

(x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3)(x + 4) = 120

Step 1: Pair the outer and inner factors: (x^2 + 5x + 4)(x^2 + 5x + 6) = 120.

Step 2: Put t = x^2 + 5x. Then (t + 4)(t + 6) = 120, so t^2 + 10t - 96 = 0, which factorizes as (t + 16)(t - 6) = 0. Hence t = 6 or t = -16.

Step 3: If t = 6, then x^2 + 5x = 6, so (x + 6)(x - 1) = 0 and x = -6 or x = 1.

Step 4: If t = -16, then x^2 + 5x + 16 = 0, and the formula gives x = (-5 +/- i sqrt(39))/2.

Related Ideas from the Review

A polynomial equation which does not change when x is replaced by 1/x is called a reciprocal equation. For example, 2x^4 - 3x^3 + 7x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0 is a reciprocal equation because its coefficients 2, -3, 7, -3, 2 are symmetric.

mcqs.q: In solving x^4 - 8x^2 - 9 = 0, which substitution is used?
mcqs.why: Putting t = x^2 turns x^4 into t^2, so the equation becomes the quadratic t^2 - 8t - 9 = 0, which can then be factorized.

mcqs.q: What are the solutions of x^4 - 8x^2 - 9 = 0?
mcqs.why: With t = x^2, (t - 9)(t + 1) = 0 gives t = 9 or t = -1. Then x^2 = 9 gives x = +/-3 and x^2 = -1 gives x = +/- i.

mcqs.q: What are the solutions of x^4 - 3x^2 - 4 = 0?
mcqs.why: Putting t = x^2 gives (t - 4)(t + 1) = 0, so t = 4 or t = -1. Hence x^2 = 4 gives x = +/-2 and x^2 = -1 gives x = +/- i.

mcqs.q: For 12x^4 - 11x^2 + 2 = 0, what values does t = x^2 take?
mcqs.why: The equation becomes 12t^2 - 11t + 2 = (3t - 2)(4t - 1) = 0, so 3t - 2 = 0 gives t = 2/3 and 4t - 1 = 0 gives t = 1/4.

mcqs.q: In 2^x + 16/2^x = 8, putting t = 2^x leads to which value of t?
mcqs.why: The equation becomes t + 16/t = 8, that is t^2 - 8t + 16 = (t - 4)^2 = 0, so t = 4, and then 2^x = 4 gives x = 2.

mcqs.q: What type of equation is 3^x + 3^(2x) = 1?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise states that 3^x + 3^(2x) = 1 is called an exponential equation because the variable appears in the powers (exponents).

mcqs.q: What is the solution of 3^x = 9?
mcqs.why: Since 9 = 3^2, the equation 3^x = 3^2 gives equal bases, so the powers must be equal and x = 2, as given in the Review Exercise.

mcqs.q: An equation unchanged when x is replaced by 1/x is called what?
mcqs.why: By definition in the Review Exercise, a polynomial equation which does not change when x is replaced by 1/x is called a reciprocal equation.

mcqs.q: In 9^(x+2) - 6 x 3^(x+1) + 1 = 0, putting t = 3^x gives t = 1/9. What is x?
mcqs.why: The equation becomes 81t^2 - 18t + 1 = (9t - 1)^2 = 0, so t = 1/9. Then 3^x = 1/9 = 3^(-2), so x = -2.

mcqs.q: For 2(x/(x+1))^2 - 5(x/(x+1)) + 2 = 0, putting t = x/(x+1) gives which t values?
mcqs.why: The equation becomes 2t^2 - 5t + 2 = (2t - 1)(t - 2) = 0, so 2t - 1 = 0 gives t = 1/2 and t - 2 = 0 gives t = 2.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.4 — Radical Equations and Extraneous Roots
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

A radical equation is an equation containing a square root (radical) of the variable. The usual method is to isolate one radical on one side and then square both sides.

Squaring can create extra solutions. A root obtained after squaring that does NOT satisfy the original equation is called an extraneous root. Extraneous roots do not satisfy the equation, so every candidate root must be checked in the original equation.

Method

Step 1: Isolate the radical on one side of the equation.

Step 2: Square both sides and solve the resulting equation, which is often quadratic.

Step 3: Check every candidate in the ORIGINAL equation.

Step 4: Keep only the values that satisfy the original equation. Those values form the solution set.

Example: One radical

x + sqrt(x + 5) = 7

Step 1: Isolate the radical: sqrt(x + 5) = 7 - x.

Step 2: Square both sides: x + 5 = 49 - 14x + x^2, so x^2 - 15x + 44 = 0, which factorizes as (x - 11)(x - 4) = 0. Hence x = 11 or x = 4.

Step 3: Check x = 11: 11 + sqrt(16) = 11 + 4 = 15, which is not 7, so x = 11 is extraneous.

Step 4: Check x = 4: 4 + sqrt(9) = 4 + 3 = 7, which is correct. The solution set is {4}.

Example: Checking both candidates

sqrt(x - 2) = 8 - x

Step 1: Square both sides: x - 2 = 64 - 16x + x^2, so x^2 - 17x + 66 = 0, which factorizes as (x - 11)(x - 6) = 0. Hence x = 11 or x = 6.

Step 2: Check x = 11: sqrt(9) = 3, but 8 - 11 = -3, and 3 is not equal to -3, so x = 11 is extraneous.

Step 3: Check x = 6: sqrt(4) = 2 and 8 - 6 = 2, so x = 6 is correct. The solution set is {6}.

Example: Two radicals

sqrt(x + 2) + sqrt(x + 7) = sqrt(6x + 13)

Step 1: Square both sides: 2x + 9 + 2sqrt(x^2 + 9x + 14) = 6x + 13.

Step 2: Isolate the remaining radical: sqrt(x^2 + 9x + 14) = 2x + 2.

Step 3: Square again: x^2 + 9x + 14 = 4x^2 + 8x + 4, so 3x^2 - x - 10 = (3x + 5)(x - 2) = 0. Hence x = -5/3 or x = 2.

Step 4: Check: x = -5/3 is extraneous. For x = 2: sqrt(4) + sqrt(9) = 2 + 3 = 5 and sqrt(25) = 5, so x = 2 is correct. The solution set is {2}.

Example: No solution

sqrt(y^2 - 3y + 9) - sqrt(y^2 - 3y + 36) = 0

Step 1: Move one radical across: sqrt(y^2 - 3y + 9) = sqrt(y^2 - 3y + 36).

Step 2: Square both sides: y^2 - 3y + 9 = y^2 - 3y + 36.

Step 3: Simplify: this gives 9 = 36, which is impossible.

Step 4: Therefore no value of y works, and the solution set is the empty set.

mcqs.q: What is an extraneous root?
options: A root that satisfies the original equation
A root obtained after squaring that does not satisfy the original equation
The larger of the two roots
mcqs.why: By definition, and as stressed in the Review Exercise true/false items, extraneous roots do NOT satisfy the original equation, so they must be rejected after checking.

mcqs.q: What is the solution set of x + sqrt(x + 5) = 7?
mcqs.why: Squaring gives x = 11 or x = 4, but checking shows 11 + sqrt(16) = 15, not 7, so 11 is extraneous and only x = 4 remains in the solution set.

mcqs.q: In sqrt(x - 2) = 8 - x, why is x = 11 rejected?
options: Because x = 11 gives 3 on the left but -3 on the right
mcqs.why: For x = 11 the left side is sqrt(9) = 3 while the right side is 8 - 11 = -3. Since 3 is not equal to -3, x = 11 is extraneous.

mcqs.q: What is the solution set of sqrt(x - 2) = 8 - x?
mcqs.why: After squaring, (x - 11)(x - 6) = 0 gives candidates 11 and 6. Only x = 6 checks correctly, since sqrt(4) = 2 = 8 - 6, so the solution set is {6}.

mcqs.q: What is the solution set of sqrt(x + 2) + sqrt(x + 7) = sqrt(6x + 13)?
mcqs.why: Squaring twice gives x = -5/3 or x = 2. Checking shows -5/3 is extraneous, while x = 2 gives 2 + 3 = 5 on both sides, so the solution set is {2}.

mcqs.q: What is the solution set of sqrt(y^2 - 3y + 9) - sqrt(y^2 - 3y + 36) = 0?
mcqs.why: Setting the radicals equal and squaring gives 9 = 36, which is impossible, so no value satisfies the equation and the solution set is the empty set.

mcqs.q: Why must candidate roots of a radical equation always be checked?
options: Because the discriminant may be negative
Because squaring both sides can introduce extraneous roots
Because every quadratic has two roots
mcqs.why: Squaring is the step that can create extra candidates. The source examples repeatedly check each candidate and reject the extraneous ones, keeping only those that satisfy the original equation.

mcqs.q: In sqrt(7 - 5x) + sqrt(13 - 5x) = 3sqrt(4 - 2x), squaring leads to candidates x = 1 and x = 3. Which is the solution?
mcqs.why: Checking shows x = 3 is outside the domain of the original radicals, while x = 1 gives sqrt(2) + sqrt(8) = 3sqrt(2), which is correct, so the solution set is {1}.

mcqs.q: For sqrt(2x^2 + 3x + 4) + sqrt(2x^2 + 3x + 9) = 5, using t = 2x^2 + 3x + 4 gives t = 4. What is the solution set?
mcqs.why: With t = 4 we get 2x^2 + 3x = 0, so x(2x + 3) = 0, giving x = 0 or x = -3/2, and the source confirms both values check out.

mcqs.q: Which statement about extraneous roots is TRUE?
options: Extraneous roots do not satisfy the equation
Every quadratic equation has an extraneous root
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise marks 'Extraneous roots do not satisfy the equation' as true and 'Extraneous roots satisfy the equation' as false, which is why they are discarded.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.1 — Identifying Congruent Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

Two triangles are congruent if all corresponding sides and corresponding angles are equal. The congruence rules used in this lesson are ASA (Angle-Side-Angle), AAS (Angle-Angle-Side, also written S.A.A), SSS and SAS. Equal angles alone (AAA) are NOT enough for congruence.

When writing a correspondence such as triangle ABC corresponding to triangle DEF, the vertices match in order: A matches D, B matches E and C matches F. So side AC corresponds to side DF, and angle MKL in triangle KLM corresponding to triangle PQR corresponds to angle QPR.

Figure for Example 1

Figure: Two triangles ABD and CBE share the vertex B. Points A and C are on opposite sides, AB is a side of the first triangle and CB is a side of the second, and the angles ABD and CBE at B are vertical angles facing each other.

Example: Proving congruence by ASA

In the figure, mAB = mCB and angle A is congruent to angle C. Prove that triangle ABD is congruent to triangle CBE.

Step 1: Angle A is congruent to angle C (given).

Step 2: AB is congruent to CB (given, since mAB = mCB).

Step 3: Angle ABD is congruent to angle CBE, because they are vertical angles.

Step 4: Two angles and the included side match, so by ASA, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle CBE.

Figure for Example 2

Figure: An angle with vertex V has two sides. Point P lies on the bisector of the angle. From P, perpendicular PQ is drawn to one side of the angle and perpendicular PR is drawn to the other side, with feet Q and R.

Example: Perpendiculars from a point on the angle bisector are equal

Prove that the perpendiculars PQ and PR from point P on the bisector to the two sides are equal.

Step 1: In triangles PQV and PRV, angle PQV = angle PRV = 90 degrees, because PQ and PR are perpendiculars.

Step 2: Angle QVP = angle RVP, because VP is the bisector of the angle.

Step 3: VP is a common side of the two triangles.

Step 4: By AAS the two triangles are congruent.

Step 5: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal, so PQ = PR.

Example: Using correspondence to find unknowns

In the figure triangle DEF is congruent to triangle PQR, with mDE = (6x + 1) cm, mEF = 8 cm, mRQ = (5y - 7) cm and mPQ = (10x - 19) cm. Find x and y.

Step 1: The correspondence is D with P, E with Q and F with R. So DE corresponds to PQ: 6x + 1 = 10x - 19.

Step 2: Solve: 20 = 4x, so x = 5.

Step 3: EF corresponds to QR, which is the same segment as RQ: 8 = 5y - 7.

Step 4: Solve: 5y = 15, so y = 3.

Useful Facts

The sum of the measures of all angles of a triangle is 180 degrees. The sum for a quadrilateral is 360 degrees. In an acute triangle all 3 angles are acute, and a triangle can have at most one obtuse angle.

mcqs.q: In the proof that triangle ABD is congruent to triangle CBE, which angles at B are used?
mcqs.why: Angles ABD and CBE face each other at the common vertex B, so they are vertical angles, and vertical angles are equal, completing the ASA proof.

mcqs.q: Which rule proves triangle ABD congruent to triangle CBE in Exercise 9.1 Q1?
mcqs.why: The matching parts are angle A with angle C, side AB with side CB, and the vertical angles at B. That is two angles and the included side, so the rule is ASA.

mcqs.q: Perpendiculars from a point on an angle bisector to the two sides are:
mcqs.why: Triangles PQV and PRV are congruent by AAS, and corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal, so the two perpendiculars PQ and PR are equal.

mcqs.q: Which congruence rule is used for the angle-bisector perpendiculars proof?
mcqs.why: The proof uses two angles (the right angles and the bisected angles) and the common side VP, which is not between those angles in the required way, so the rule stated in the source is AAS.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a suitable rule for congruence of two triangles?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise states that A.A.A is not suitable, because equal angles alone do not fix the size of a triangle, so the triangles need not be congruent.

mcqs.q: If triangle DEF is congruent to triangle PQR with DE = (6x+1) and PQ = (10x-19), what is x?
mcqs.why: By correspondence D matches P and E matches Q, so DE = PQ: 6x + 1 = 10x - 19 gives 20 = 4x, hence x = 5.

mcqs.q: In the same congruence, if EF = 8 cm and RQ = (5y - 7) cm, what is y?
mcqs.why: EF corresponds to QR, the same as RQ, so 8 = 5y - 7. Then 5y = 15, which gives y = 3 after dividing by 5.

mcqs.q: If triangle ABC corresponds to triangle DEF, side AC corresponds to which side?
mcqs.why: In the correspondence A-B-C matches D-E-F in order, so A matches D and C matches F. Therefore side AC corresponds to side DF, as in the Review Exercise.

mcqs.q: What is the sum of the measures of all angles of a triangle?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise marks the statement that the sum is 270 degrees as false, because the angles of any triangle always add up to 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC congruent to triangle DEF, if angle A = 120 degrees and angle B = 30 degrees, what is angle F?
mcqs.why: First angle C = 180 - 120 - 30 = 30 degrees. By correspondence C matches F, so angle F = angle C = 30 degrees.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.2 — Properties of an Isosceles Triangle
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. The angles opposite the equal sides, called the base angles, are equal. In this lesson, isosceles triangles are also recognised the other way: if two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal and the triangle is isosceles.

A useful angle fact is that the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees:

angle A + angle B + angle C = 180 degrees

Figure for Example 1

Figure: Triangle ABC has vertex A at the top, with B and C on the base. From B a perpendicular BD is drawn to side AC, meeting AC at D, so triangle BDC is formed on the right side.

Example: Showing a right triangle is isosceles

In triangle ABC, m angle A = 35 degrees and m angle B = 100 degrees, and BD is perpendicular to AC. Prove that triangle BDC is isosceles.

Step 1: Find angle C of triangle ABC: angle C = 180 - 35 - 100 = 45 degrees.

Step 2: In triangle BDC, angle BDC = 90 degrees because BD is perpendicular to AC.

Step 3: Find angle DBC: angle DBC = 180 - 90 - 45 = 45 degrees.

Step 4: Since angle DBC = angle C = 45 degrees, the sides opposite them are equal, DC = DB.

Step 5: Therefore triangle BDC is an isosceles triangle.

Figure for Example 2

Figure: Triangle DBC is a right triangle with the right angle at D, because CD is perpendicular to AB. Vertex B is on one side and C is above D.

Example: A second isosceles right triangle

In triangle ABC, m angle B = 45 degrees and CD is perpendicular to AB. Prove that triangle DBC is isosceles.

Step 1: In triangle DBC, angle CDB = 90 degrees because CD is perpendicular to AB.

Step 2: Angle B is given as 45 degrees.

Step 3: Find angle DCB: angle DCB = 180 - 90 - 45 = 45 degrees.

Step 4: Since angle DCB = angle B = 45 degrees, the opposite sides are equal: DB = DC.

Step 5: Therefore triangle DBC is an isosceles triangle.

Figure for Example 3

Figure: Triangle ABC has vertex A at the top and base BC below. Segment AD goes from A down to BC, bisects angle A, and meets BC at right angles at D.

Example: Angle bisector perpendicular to the opposite side

Prove: if the bisector of any angle of a triangle is perpendicular to the opposite side, then the triangle is isosceles.

Step 1: Let AD bisect angle A and meet BC at D, with AD perpendicular to BC.

Step 2: In triangles ABD and ACD, angle BAD = angle CAD, because AD bisects angle A.

Step 3: AD is a common side.

Step 4: Angle ADB = angle ADC = 90 degrees, because AD is perpendicular to BC.

Step 5: By ASA the two triangles are congruent, so AB = AC.

Step 6: Since two sides are equal, triangle ABC is an isosceles triangle.

Note: In an isosceles triangle only the two base angles are equal; it is false that all angles of an isosceles triangle are of the same measure. If each angle of a triangle measures 60 degrees, the triangle is equilateral.

mcqs.q: In an isosceles triangle, which angles are equal?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise confirms that in an isosceles triangle the base angles are equal, and it is false that all angles are of the same measure.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC with angle A = 35 degrees and angle B = 100 degrees, what is angle C?
mcqs.why: The angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees, so angle C = 180 - 35 - 100 = 45 degrees, as calculated in the source solution.

mcqs.q: In triangle BDC with right angle at D and angle C = 45 degrees, what is angle DBC?
mcqs.why: Angle DBC = 180 - 90 - 45 = 45 degrees. This equals angle C, which is exactly why triangle BDC is isosceles.

mcqs.q: Why is triangle BDC isosceles in Exercise 9.2 Q1?
options: Because angle DBC = angle C, so DC = DB
Because all its sides are equal
Because BD is the longest side
mcqs.why: Equal angles have equal opposite sides. Since angle DBC and angle C are both 45 degrees, the sides opposite them, DC and DB, are equal, making the triangle isosceles.

mcqs.q: If the bisector of an angle of a triangle is perpendicular to the opposite side, the triangle is:
mcqs.why: Triangles ABD and ACD are congruent by ASA, which gives AB = AC. A triangle with two equal sides is an isosceles triangle.

mcqs.q: In the bisector proof, which congruence rule is applied to triangles ABD and ACD?
mcqs.why: The matching parts are angle BAD = angle CAD, the common side AD, and the right angles at D. That is angle-side-angle with the side between the angles, so ASA.

mcqs.q: In triangle DBC, right-angled at D, if angle B = 45 degrees then angle DCB equals:
mcqs.why: Angle DCB = 180 - 90 - 45 = 45 degrees, using the angle sum of a triangle, which matches the source working step by step.

mcqs.q: In triangle DBC of Exercise 9.2 Q3, which sides are equal?
mcqs.why: Because angle DCB = angle B = 45 degrees, the sides opposite these equal angles are equal, and the source states this as DB = DC.

mcqs.q: If each angle of a triangle measures 60 degrees, the triangle is:
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise fill-in states that if each angle measures 60 degrees the triangle is equilateral, with all sides and all angles equal.

mcqs.q: How many obtuse angles can a triangle have at most?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise marks 'In a triangle there are two obtuse angles' as false, because two obtuse angles alone would already exceed 180 degrees, so at most one is possible.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.3 — Median and Perpendicular Bisector in an Isosceles Triangle
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

In an isosceles triangle, the line from the vertex to the midpoint of the base does three jobs: it is a median, it bisects the vertex angle, and it is perpendicular to the base. Also, a point that is equidistant from the two ends of a segment lies on the perpendicular bisector of that segment.

Figure for Example 1

Figure: Isosceles triangle ABC has equal sides AB and AC meeting at vertex A, and base BC below. Point D is the midpoint of BC, and segment AD joins the vertex to the midpoint of the base.

Example: Median to the base bisects the angle and is perpendicular

ABC is an isosceles triangle and D is the midpoint of its base BC. Prove that AD bisects angle A and AD is perpendicular to BC.

Step 1: In triangles ABD and ACD, AB = AC because the triangle is isosceles.

Step 2: BD = DC, because D is the midpoint of BC.

Step 3: AD is a common side.

Step 4: By SSS the two triangles are congruent.

Step 5: Therefore angle BAD = angle CAD, which means AD is the bisector of angle A.

Step 6: Also angle ADB = angle ADC. These two angles form a linear pair adding to 180 degrees, so each is 90 degrees.

Step 7: Therefore AD is perpendicular to BC.

Figure for Example 2

Figure: Two isosceles triangles ABC and DBC stand on the same base BC, with vertices A and D on the same line through the middle of BC. Segment AD is drawn joining the two vertices.

Example: AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC

Triangles ABC and DBC are isosceles triangles on the common base BC. Prove that AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC.

Step 1: AB = AC, because triangle ABC is isosceles, so A is equidistant from B and C.

Step 2: DB = DC, because triangle DBC is isosceles, so D is also equidistant from B and C.

Step 3: Points equidistant from B and C lie on the perpendicular bisector of BC.

Step 4: Both A and D lie on that perpendicular bisector, so the line AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC.

Example: Medians to the equal sides are equal

This is the statement as printed: the medians of an isosceles triangle (to the equal sides) are equal. In isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC, let M be the midpoint of AB and N the midpoint of AC.

Step 1: BM = CN, because they are halves of the equal sides AB and AC.

Step 2: In triangles BCM and CBN, BC is a common side.

Step 3: Angle B = angle C, because they are the base angles of the isosceles triangle.

Step 4: By SAS the two triangles are congruent.

Step 5: Therefore CM = BN, that is, the medians to the equal sides are equal.

Example: Midpoints in a square

In square PQRS, X, Y and Z are the midpoints of sides PQ, QR and RS. The source proves triangle PXY congruent to triangle SZY by SSS: PX = SZ as halves of equal sides, while PY = SY and XY = ZY are each found by Pythagoras in equal right triangles.

mcqs.q: In isosceles triangle ABC with D the midpoint of base BC, which rule proves triangles ABD and ACD congruent?
mcqs.why: The three matching sides are AB = AC, BD = DC and the common side AD, so all three sides match and the rule is SSS, as in the source proof.

mcqs.q: In that proof, why is AD perpendicular to BC?
options: Because D is any point on BC
Because AD is the longest side
Because angles ADB and ADC are equal and form a linear pair, so each is 90 degrees
mcqs.why: Congruence gives angle ADB = angle ADC. They sit on a straight line and add to 180 degrees, so each must be 90 degrees, making AD perpendicular to BC.

mcqs.q: In that proof, AD is also the bisector of which angle?
mcqs.why: Congruence of triangles ABD and ACD gives angle BAD = angle CAD, so AD splits angle A into two equal parts and is the bisector of angle A.

mcqs.q: Two isosceles triangles ABC and DBC share base BC. AD is what for BC?
options: An altitude only of one triangle
mcqs.why: Both A and D are equidistant from B and C, and such points lie on the perpendicular bisector of BC, so the line AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC.

mcqs.q: A point equidistant from the ends B and C of a segment lies on:
mcqs.why: This is the key fact used in the source proof: any point equally distant from B and C lies on the perpendicular bisector of segment BC.

mcqs.q: In an isosceles triangle, the medians to the equal sides are:
mcqs.why: Triangles BCM and CBN are congruent by SAS, so their corresponding sides CM and BN, the medians to the equal sides, must be equal.

mcqs.q: Which rule is used to prove the medians to the equal sides are equal?
mcqs.why: The proof uses BC common, base angles B = C, and BM = CN. Those are two sides and the included angle pattern applied as SAS in the source solution.

mcqs.q: Why is BM = CN in the medians proof?
options: Because M and N are vertices
Because they are halves of the equal sides AB and AC
mcqs.why: M is the midpoint of AB and N is the midpoint of AC, and since AB = AC in the isosceles triangle, their halves BM and CN are also equal.

mcqs.q: In square PQRS, triangle PXY is proved congruent to triangle SZY by which rule?
mcqs.why: All three sides match: PX = SZ directly, and PY = SY and XY = ZY by Pythagoras in equal right triangles, so the congruence is by SSS.

mcqs.q: If angle A is congruent to angle B in triangle ABC, the bisector of which angle divides it into two congruent triangles?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise answer is angle C: the bisector from the vertex between the two equal base angles splits the isosceles triangle into two congruent halves.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.4 — Altitude and Median in an Isosceles Triangle
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

In an isosceles triangle, the median to the base, the bisector of the vertex angle and the altitude to the base are all the same line. Altitudes (perpendiculars) drawn from the base vertices to the opposite sides are also equal. The area fact used here is:

Area of a triangle = (1/2) x base x altitude

Figure for Example 1

Figure: Isosceles triangle ABC has equal sides AB and AC and base BC. From B a perpendicular BD is drawn to side AC, and from C a perpendicular CE is drawn to side AB.

Example: Perpendiculars from the base vertices are equal

In isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC, BD is perpendicular to AC and CE is perpendicular to AB. Prove that BD = CE.

Step 1: In triangles BCE and CBD, angle BEC = angle CDB = 90 degrees, because the segments are perpendiculars.

Step 2: Angle EBC = angle DCB, because they are the base angles of the isosceles triangle.

Step 3: BC is a common side.

Step 4: By AAS the two triangles are congruent.

Step 5: Therefore CE = BD, so the two perpendiculars are equal.

Figure for Example 2

Figure: Isosceles triangle ABC with vertex A at the top and base BC below. Point D is the midpoint of BC and segment AD is drawn from A to D.

Example: Median, bisector and altitude are the same line

Prove that in an isosceles triangle the median to the base, the bisector of the vertex angle and the altitude to the base are the same line.

Step 1: Let D be the midpoint of BC. Then triangles ABD and ACD are congruent by SSS, as shown in Exercise 9.3.

Step 2: From the congruence, angle BAD = angle CAD, so AD is the bisector of the vertex angle.

Step 3: Also angle ADB = angle ADC = 90 degrees, so AD is perpendicular to the base, that is, AD is the altitude.

Step 4: AD is by construction the median to the base.

Step 5: Therefore the median, the bisector and the altitude are one and the same line AD.

Example: Bisector perpendicular to the opposite side (again)

If AD bisects angle A and AD is perpendicular to BC, then in triangles ABD and ACD: angle BAD = angle CAD, AD is common, and angle ADB = angle ADC = 90 degrees. By ASA the triangles are congruent, so AB = AC and the triangle is isosceles.

Example: Equal altitudes

Prove the printed result about equal altitudes using area.

Step 1: Write the area three ways, once with each side as base: Area = (1/2) x base x altitude for each choice of base.

Step 2: If all three altitudes are equal, then for the areas to stay equal, all three bases (the sides) must also be equal.

Step 3: A triangle with all sides equal is equilateral, and an equilateral triangle is also isosceles.

mcqs.q: In an isosceles triangle, the perpendiculars from the base vertices to the opposite sides are:
mcqs.why: Triangles BCE and CBD are congruent by AAS, so their corresponding sides CE and BD, which are those perpendiculars, are equal to each other.

mcqs.q: Which rule proves triangles BCE and CBD congruent in the perpendiculars proof?
mcqs.why: The matching parts are the two right angles, the base angles, and the common side BC, which the source identifies as the AAS rule.

mcqs.q: In an isosceles triangle, the median to the base, the vertex-angle bisector and the altitude to the base are:
mcqs.why: From triangles ABD congruent to ACD by SSS, segment AD is at once the median, the bisector of the vertex angle and the perpendicular altitude to the base.

mcqs.q: In the same-line proof, AD is perpendicular to the base because:
options: Angles ADB and ADC are each 90 degrees
mcqs.why: Congruence gives angle ADB = angle ADC, and as a linear pair they add to 180 degrees, so each is 90 degrees and AD is perpendicular, making it the altitude.

mcqs.q: Which side is common in triangles BCE and CBD?
mcqs.why: Both triangles stand on the base BC of the isosceles triangle, so BC is the side shared by triangles BCE and CBD in the proof.

mcqs.q: If the bisector of an angle is perpendicular to the opposite side, then by ASA we first conclude:
options: The triangles ABD and ACD are congruent
mcqs.why: Angle BAD = angle CAD, AD common, and both angles at D are 90 degrees give ASA congruence of triangles ABD and ACD, from which AB = AC follows.

mcqs.q: The area of a triangle is given by which formula?
mcqs.why: The source proof for equal altitudes starts from Area = (1/2) x base x altitude, applied with each side in turn as the base.

mcqs.q: If all three altitudes of a triangle are equal, the source concludes the sides are:
mcqs.why: With equal altitudes and the same area from (1/2) x base x altitude, the bases must be equal too, so all three sides are equal.

mcqs.q: A triangle with all three sides equal, as concluded in that proof, is called:
mcqs.why: The source states the triangle is equilateral when all sides are equal, and notes that an equilateral triangle is also counted as isosceles.

mcqs.q: In the perpendiculars proof, angles BEC and CDB are each:
mcqs.why: BD is perpendicular to AC and CE is perpendicular to AB, so the angles where they meet those sides, angles CDB and BEC, are right angles of 90 degrees.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1 — Properties of a Parallelogram
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. Its key properties are: opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal, consecutive (interior angles on any side) are supplementary, and the diagonals bisect each other.

angle A + angle B = 180 degrees

Supplementary means two angles add up to 180 degrees, that is, 2 right angles. The sum of the interior angles of any quadrilateral is 360 degrees, that is, 4 right angles.

Figure for Examples

Figure: Parallelogram ABCD goes around in order, with AB at the top, BC on the right, CD at the bottom and DA on the left. Side AD is parallel to side BC and side AB is parallel to side CD.

Example: Interior angles on any side are supplementary

Prove that the interior angles on any side of a parallelogram are supplementary.

Step 1: In parallelogram ABCD, AD is parallel to BC and AB is a transversal cutting them.

Step 2: Angles A and B are consecutive interior angles on the same side of the transversal.

Step 3: Consecutive interior angles between parallel lines are supplementary, so angle A + angle B = 180 degrees.

Step 4: The same argument works on every side, so the angles on every side are supplementary.

Example: Opposite angles are equal

Prove that the opposite angles of any parallelogram are equal.

Step 1: From the previous result, angle A + angle B = 180 degrees.

Step 2: Also angle B + angle C = 180 degrees, applying the same result on the next side.

Step 3: Both angle A and angle C make 180 degrees with angle B, so angle A = angle C.

Step 4: In the same way, angle B = angle D. Therefore opposite angles are equal.

Example: Bisectors of two angles on the same side meet at a right angle

Prove that the bisectors of two angles on the same side of a parallelogram intersect at a right angle.

Step 1: Angle A + angle B = 180 degrees, because they are supplementary.

Step 2: Let the two bisectors meet at P. In triangle APB, angle PAB + angle PBA = (1/2)(angle A + angle B), because each is half of its angle.

Step 3: So angle PAB + angle PBA = (1/2)(180 degrees) = 90 degrees.

Step 4: Then angle APB = 180 - 90 = 90 degrees, so the bisectors are perpendicular to each other.

Example: Joining the midpoints of opposite sides

In parallelogram ABCD, M is the midpoint of AD and N is the midpoint of BC. Then AM = BN, as halves of equal opposite sides, and AM is parallel to BN, so AMNB is a parallelogram. Hence MN is parallel to AB and also parallel to CD.

mcqs.q: In a parallelogram, the interior angles on any side are:
mcqs.why: AD is parallel to BC with AB as transversal, so angles A and B are consecutive interior angles and add to 180 degrees, meaning they are supplementary.

mcqs.q: The opposite angles of a parallelogram are:
mcqs.why: Since angle A + angle B = 180 and angle B + angle C = 180, it follows that angle A = angle C, and similarly angle B = angle D, so opposite angles are equal.

mcqs.q: The bisectors of two angles on the same side of a parallelogram intersect at:
mcqs.why: Half of angle A plus half of angle B equals half of 180 degrees, which is 90 degrees, leaving angle APB = 90 degrees in triangle APB.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, angle A + angle B equals:
mcqs.why: Angles A and B are consecutive interior angles between the parallel sides AD and BC, and such angles are supplementary, adding to 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are:
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise fill-in states directly that in a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, a basic property used throughout this unit.

mcqs.q: The diagonals of a parallelogram ______ each other.
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise states that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, each diagonal cutting the other into two equal parts.

mcqs.q: The consecutive angles of a parallelogram are:
mcqs.why: Consecutive angles lie on the same side of the parallelogram, and by the theorem of this exercise they are supplementary, adding to 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, if angle A + angle C = 130 degrees, what is angle C?
mcqs.why: Opposite angles are equal, so angle A = angle C and 2 x angle C = 130 degrees, giving angle C = 65 degrees, as in the Review Exercise.

mcqs.q: The line joining the midpoints of two opposite sides of a parallelogram is:
options: Parallel to the other two sides
mcqs.why: With M and N the midpoints, AM = BN and AM parallel to BN makes AMNB a parallelogram, so MN is parallel to AB and to CD, the other two sides.

mcqs.q: The sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is:
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise confirms the sum is 360 degrees, which is 4 right angles, for any quadrilateral including a parallelogram.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2 — Conditions for a Parallelogram
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

This lesson gives tests (conditions) that guarantee a quadrilateral is a parallelogram: opposite angles equal; diagonals bisecting each other; angles on every side supplementary. Also, a diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.

Figure for Examples

Figure: Quadrilateral ABCD goes around in order. Its diagonals AC and BD cross inside at point O, with AO on one part of one diagonal and OC on the other part.

Example: Opposite angles equal implies a parallelogram

Prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram if its opposite angles are equal.

Step 1: Let angle A = angle C and angle B = angle D.

Step 2: The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360 degrees, so 2 angle A + 2 angle B = 360 degrees.

Step 3: Divide by 2: angle A + angle B = 180 degrees. Supplementary consecutive angles mean AD is parallel to BC.

Step 4: Similarly angle B + angle C = 180 degrees, so AB is parallel to CD.

Step 5: Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so ABCD is a parallelogram.

Example: Diagonals bisecting each other implies a parallelogram

Prove that a quadrilateral is a parallelogram if its diagonals bisect each other.

Step 1: The diagonals AC and BD meet at O with AO = OC and BO = OD.

Step 2: Angle AOB = angle COD, because they are vertical angles, so triangle AOB is congruent to triangle COD by SAS.

Step 3: Therefore AB = CD and angle OAB = angle OCD, which gives AB parallel to CD by alternate angles.

Step 4: In the same way AD is parallel to BC.

Step 5: Therefore ABCD is a parallelogram.

Example: A diagonal forms congruent triangles

If ABCD is a parallelogram, its diagonals form congruent triangles. Diagonal AC divides it into triangles ABC and CDA.

Step 1: AB = CD, because opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.

Step 2: BC = AD, for the same reason.

Step 3: AC is a common side.

Step 4: By SSS, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle CDA. Similarly diagonal BD gives triangle ABD congruent to triangle CDB.

Example: Supplementary angles on every side

If the angles on every side of a quadrilateral are supplementary, it is a parallelogram: angle A + angle B = 180 degrees gives AD parallel to BC, and angle B + angle C = 180 degrees gives AB parallel to CD, so both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.

mcqs.q: A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite angles equal is a:
mcqs.why: From angle A = angle C and angle B = angle D, the angle sum gives angle A + angle B = 180 degrees, forcing both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so it is a parallelogram.

mcqs.q: If the diagonals of a quadrilateral bisect each other, then it is a:
mcqs.why: Triangles AOB and COD are congruent by SAS using the bisected diagonals and vertical angles, giving both pairs of opposite sides parallel, hence a parallelogram.

mcqs.q: In the diagonals proof, triangles AOB and COD are congruent by:
mcqs.why: AO = OC and BO = OD because the diagonals bisect each other, and the included angles AOB and COD are vertical angles, so the rule is SAS.

mcqs.q: In that proof, AB is parallel to CD because of:
options: Alternate angles OAB and OCD being equal
mcqs.why: Congruence gives angle OAB = angle OCD. These are alternate angles for lines AB and CD cut by AC, and equal alternate angles mean the lines are parallel.

mcqs.q: A diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into:
mcqs.why: Diagonal AC gives triangles ABC and CDA with AB = CD, BC = AD and AC common, so by SSS the two triangles are congruent.

mcqs.q: Which rule proves triangle ABC congruent to triangle CDA in a parallelogram?
mcqs.why: All three sides match: AB = CD and BC = AD as opposite sides of the parallelogram, and AC is common to both triangles, so the rule is SSS.

mcqs.q: If angles on every side of a quadrilateral are supplementary, the quadrilateral is a:
mcqs.why: Angle A + angle B = 180 degrees makes AD parallel to BC, and angle B + angle C = 180 degrees makes AB parallel to CD, so it is a parallelogram.

mcqs.q: Angle A + angle B = 180 degrees in a quadrilateral tells us that:
mcqs.why: Supplementary consecutive interior angles mean the lines forming them are parallel; for angles A and B the relevant parallel sides are AD and BC, as used in the source proofs.

mcqs.q: If opposite angles of a quadrilateral are equal and none is obtuse, the Review Exercise says it is a:
mcqs.why: Equal opposite angles make it a parallelogram first, and with no obtuse angle every angle must be 90 degrees, which makes the parallelogram a rectangle.

mcqs.q: The diagonal of which figure does NOT divide it into two congruent triangles?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise of Unit 9 gives trapezium as the answer: its diagonal does not in general create two congruent triangles, unlike rectangle, parallelogram and square.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3 — The Mid-Point Theorem
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

Mid-Point Theorem (Midsegment Theorem): the segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and half as long as the third side:

midsegment = (1/2) x third side

Converse: a line through the midpoint of one side of a triangle parallel to a second side bisects the third side.

Figure for Examples

Figure: Triangle ABC has vertex A at the top, B at the bottom left and C at the bottom right. Points on AB and AC are their midpoints, and the segment joining those midpoints runs across the middle of the triangle, parallel to base BC.

Example: Finding the third side

The midpoints of two sides of a triangle are joined and the joining segment is 4 cm. Find the third side.

Step 1: By the midsegment theorem, the joining segment is half the third side.

Step 2: So third side = 2 x 4 cm.

Step 3: Therefore the third side is 8 cm.

In the same way, from the Review Exercise, if the segment joining the midpoints of AB and AC is 3.5 cm, then BC = 2 x 3.5 = 7 cm.

Example: Converse of the mid-point theorem

Prove that a line through the midpoint of one side of a triangle parallel to the second side bisects the third side.

Step 1: In triangle ABC, let D be the midpoint of AB and let DE be parallel to BC, meeting AC at E.

Step 2: From similar triangles, AD/AB = AE/AC.

Step 3: Since D is the midpoint, AD/AB = 1/2, so 1/2 = AE/AC.

Step 4: Therefore AE = (1/2)AC, which means E is the midpoint of AC, so the line bisects the third side.

Example: Midpoints of a quadrilateral form a parallelogram

Joining the midpoints of the four sides of a quadrilateral in order forms a parallelogram.

Step 1: In quadrilateral ABCD, let P, Q, R, S be the midpoints of AB, BC, CD, DA.

Step 2: In triangle ABC, PQ is parallel to AC and PQ = (1/2)AC. In triangle CDA, SR is parallel to AC and SR = (1/2)AC. So PQ is parallel and equal to SR.

Step 3: In the same way, from triangles BCD and DAB, QR is parallel and equal to PS, with QR = PS = (1/2)BD.

Step 4: Both pairs of opposite sides of PQRS are parallel and equal, so PQRS is a parallelogram.

Step 5: In a parallelogram the diagonals bisect each other, so the segments joining the midpoints of opposite sides of the quadrilateral bisect each other.

Example: Four congruent small triangles

Joining the midpoints of the three sides of a triangle forms four small triangles. By the midsegment theorem, every side of each small triangle is half of a corresponding side of the big triangle, so all four small triangles have the same three side lengths and are congruent by SSS.

mcqs.q: The segment joining the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is ______ the third side.
mcqs.why: By the midsegment theorem the joining segment is half the third side, which is why a 4 cm segment gives a third side of 8 cm.

mcqs.q: If the midsegment joining the midpoints of two sides is 4 cm, the third side is:
mcqs.why: The third side is twice the midsegment, so third side = 2 x 4 cm = 8 cm, exactly as worked in the source example.

mcqs.q: The segment joining the midpoints of AB and AC is 3.5 cm. Then BC is:
mcqs.why: BC is the third side, so BC = 2 x 3.5 cm = 7 cm. This is the Review Exercise question and its answer is 7 cm.

mcqs.q: The midsegment joining two midpoints of a triangle is also ______ the third side.
mcqs.why: The mid-point theorem states the joining segment is parallel to the third side as well as half its length, and both facts are used in every proof of this exercise.

mcqs.q: A line through the midpoint of one side, parallel to a second side, does what to the third side?
mcqs.why: From AD/AB = AE/AC and AD/AB = 1/2, we get AE = (1/2)AC, so the meeting point is the midpoint: the line bisects the third side.

mcqs.q: Joining the midpoints of the four sides of a quadrilateral in order forms a:
mcqs.why: PQ and SR are both parallel to AC and equal to (1/2)AC, and QR and PS are both (1/2)BD, so PQRS has both pairs of opposite sides parallel: a parallelogram.

mcqs.q: The segments joining the midpoints of opposite sides of a quadrilateral:
mcqs.why: Those segments are the diagonals of the midpoint parallelogram PQRS, and diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, as proved in the source.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, PQ joining midpoints on two sides with diagonal AC satisfies:
options: PQ = (1/2) AC and PQ parallel to AC
mcqs.why: Applying the midsegment theorem in triangle ABC with AC as the third side gives PQ parallel to AC and PQ equal to half of AC.

mcqs.q: Joining the midpoints of the three sides of a triangle forms four small triangles that are:
mcqs.why: Each small triangle has sides that are halves of the big triangle's sides, so all four have the same three lengths and are congruent by SSS.

mcqs.q: Which rule shows the four small midpoint triangles are congruent?
mcqs.why: Their corresponding sides are all equal (each is half of a side of the original triangle), and equal three sides is the SSS congruence rule.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.4 — Medians and the Centroid
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

A median of a triangle joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. A triangle has three medians. The three medians meet at a single point called the centroid. The centroid is the common point of the medians of the triangle, and it divides each median in the ratio 2:1, the part towards the vertex being twice the part towards the side:

vertex part : side part = 2 : 1

Figure for Examples

Figure: Triangle PQR has vertices P, Q and R. Points on the opposite sides are the midpoints, and the three medians PB, QC and RA are drawn inside, all crossing at one interior point labelled G.

Example: The centroid divides the median in ratio 2:1

The medians PB, QC and RA of triangle PQR meet at G. Prove that G is the centroid.

Step 1: PB, QC and RA are medians, so each joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

Step 2: The three medians of a triangle meet at a single point.

Step 3: That single meeting point is called the centroid.

Step 4: By the centroid theorem, G divides each median in the ratio 2:1, so G is the centroid.

Example: Using the 2:1 ratio

In the figure, the length of GR is 2 cm. Find the length of AG, where RA is a median and G is the centroid on it.

Step 1: G divides the median RA in the ratio RG : GA = 2 : 1.

Step 2: GR is the vertex part, equal to 2 cm, corresponding to the 2 in the ratio.

Step 3: So GA is the 1 part: AG = 2 cm / 2 = 1 cm.

In the same way, from the Review Exercise: medians AD and BE meet at G with GD = 1.7 cm, so AG = 2 x 1.7 = 3.4 cm.

Example: Equal medians and an isosceles triangle

Prove that if (two of) the three medians of a triangle are equal in the source argument, extended to all three, the conclusion drawn is that the triangle is isosceles. The source uses the median-length (Apollonius) formulas:

m_a^2 = (2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2) / 4

m_b^2 = (2a^2 + 2c^2 - b^2) / 4

Step 1: If m_a = m_b, then 2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2 = 2a^2 + 2c^2 - b^2.

Step 2: Simplify: 3b^2 = 3a^2, so a^2 = b^2 and a = b.

Step 3: Two sides are equal, therefore the triangle is isosceles.

mcqs.q: The three medians of a triangle meet at a point called the:
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise confirms the centroid is the common point of the medians of the triangle, where all three medians meet at a single point.

mcqs.q: How many medians does a triangle have?
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise fill-in states that in a triangle the medians are three, one drawn from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

mcqs.q: The centroid divides each median in the ratio:
mcqs.why: By the centroid theorem, G divides each median in the ratio 2:1, with the vertex part twice as long as the part towards the side.

mcqs.q: If GR = 2 cm on median RA with centroid G, what is AG?
mcqs.why: RG : GA = 2 : 1 and GR = 2 cm is the 2-part, so the 1-part GA must be half of that, namely AG = 1 cm.

mcqs.q: Medians AD and BE meet at G. If GD = 1.7 cm, then AG is:
mcqs.why: On median AD, AG is the vertex part and GD the side part, with AG = 2 x GD = 2 x 1.7 = 3.4 cm, the Review Exercise answer.

mcqs.q: The medians of a triangle are described in the Review Exercise as:
mcqs.why: The fill-in answer is that the medians of a triangle are concurrent at the centroid, meaning all three pass through that one point.

mcqs.q: If two medians satisfy m_a = m_b in the Apollonius formulas, the proof obtains:
mcqs.why: Setting the formulas equal gives 2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2 = 2a^2 + 2c^2 - b^2, which simplifies to 3b^2 = 3a^2, hence a = b.

mcqs.q: From a = b in that proof, the triangle is concluded to be:
mcqs.why: Two equal sides, a = b, is exactly the condition for an isosceles triangle, which is the conclusion stated in the source solution.

mcqs.q: Which formula is the median-length formula for m_a in the source?
mcqs.why: The source (Apollonius) formula is m_a^2 = (2b^2 + 2c^2 - a^2)/4, and the matching formula for m_b is used alongside it in the proof.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the centroid a common point of?
options: The bisectors of the angles only
mcqs.why: The Review Exercise multiple-choice answer is (a) the medians of the triangle: the centroid is defined as their common meeting point.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.5 — Results about Mid-Points
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

This lesson collects further results about mid-points: the angles of the midpoint triangle equal those of the original triangle; the midline of a trapezium is parallel to the parallel sides and equals half their sum; and the midsegment of a triangle bisects every segment from the opposite vertex to the base.

trapezium midline = (1/2)(sum of the two parallel sides)

Figure for Example 1

Figure: A large triangle has its three side midpoints joined to form a smaller upside-down triangle in the middle, with three corner small triangles around it, making four small triangles in total.

Example: Angles of the new triangle

Prove that the angles of the new triangle formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of any triangle are equal to those of the original triangle.

Step 1: Joining the midpoints forms four small triangles.

Step 2: The four small triangles are congruent to each other, as shown in Exercise 10.3.

Step 3: They are also similar to the original triangle by SSS similarity, with ratio 1:2.

Step 4: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles, so the angles of the new (middle) triangle equal the angles of the original triangle.

Figure for Example 2

Figure: Trapezium ABCD has AB parallel to CD, with AB the shorter top side and CD the longer bottom side. M is the midpoint of the non-parallel side AD and N is the midpoint of the non-parallel side BC. Diagonal AC crosses segment MN at point P.

Example: Midline of a trapezium

Prove that the segment joining the midpoints of the non-parallel sides of a trapezium is parallel to the other two sides and equal to half the sum of those two sides.

Step 1: In trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to CD, let M be the midpoint of AD and N the midpoint of BC. Draw diagonal AC meeting MN at P.

Step 2: In triangle ACD, M is the midpoint of AD and MP is parallel to CD, so MP = (1/2)CD and MP is parallel to CD.

Step 3: In triangle ABC, P and N give PN = (1/2)AB and PN is parallel to AB.

Step 4: Combine the parts: MN = MP + PN = (1/2)CD + (1/2)AB = (1/2)(AB + CD).

Step 5: Since both parts are parallel to AB and CD, MN is parallel to AB and to CD.

Figure for Example 3

Figure: Triangle ABC has vertex A at the top and base BC below. M is the midpoint of AB and N is the midpoint of AC, with midsegment MN across the middle. A segment AD goes from A to a point D on BC and crosses MN at point P.

Example: The midsegment bisects a segment from the vertex

Prove that every line segment drawn from the vertex of any triangle to the base is bisected by the segment joining the midpoints of the other two sides.

Step 1: In triangle ABC, let M be the midpoint of AB and N the midpoint of AC, so MN is the midsegment. Let AD be any segment from A to a point D on BC, meeting MN at P.

Step 2: Consider triangle ABD. M is the midpoint of AB.

Step 3: MP is part of the midsegment, so MP is parallel to BD (part of the base).

Step 4: By the converse of the mid-point theorem, a line through the midpoint parallel to the base bisects the third side, so P is the midpoint of AD.

Step 5: Therefore MN bisects AD, as required.

mcqs.q: The angles of the triangle formed by joining the midpoints of a triangle's sides are ______ the original triangle's angles.
mcqs.why: The midpoint triangles are similar to the original with ratio 1:2 by SSS similarity, and similar triangles have equal corresponding angles.

mcqs.q: The four small midpoint triangles are similar to the original triangle with which ratio?
mcqs.why: Every side of a small triangle is half the corresponding side of the original, so the similarity ratio of small to original is 1:2, as stated in the source.

mcqs.q: The segment joining the midpoints of the non-parallel sides of a trapezium is ______ the parallel sides.
mcqs.why: Both parts MP and PN are parallel to AB and CD by the mid-point theorem, so the whole segment MN is parallel to the other two sides.

mcqs.q: The length of that trapezium midline equals:
mcqs.why: MN = MP + PN = (1/2)CD + (1/2)AB = (1/2)(AB + CD), half the sum of the two parallel sides, exactly as proved in the source.

mcqs.q: In the trapezium proof, MP in triangle ACD equals:
mcqs.why: M is the midpoint of AD and MP is parallel to CD, so by the mid-point theorem MP is half of the third side CD, that is MP = (1/2)CD.

mcqs.q: In the trapezium proof, PN in triangle ABC equals:
mcqs.why: In triangle ABC the segment PN joins midpoint positions parallel to AB, so PN = (1/2)AB, and adding MP gives the half-sum formula for MN.

mcqs.q: Every segment from a triangle's vertex to the base is ______ by the midsegment joining the midpoints of the other two sides.
mcqs.why: In triangle ABD, M is the midpoint of AB and MP is parallel to BD, so P must be the midpoint of AD: the midsegment bisects the vertex segment.

mcqs.q: In that proof, P is the midpoint of AD because of:
options: The converse of the mid-point theorem
mcqs.why: A line through the midpoint of one side parallel to another side bisects the third side: that converse result, applied in triangle ABD, makes P the midpoint of AD.

mcqs.q: Which segment is the midsegment in the vertex-segment proof?
options: MN joining the midpoints of AB and AC
mcqs.why: M and N are the midpoints of AB and AC, so the segment joining them, MN, is the midsegment that crosses and bisects AD at P.

mcqs.q: If a trapezium has parallel sides AB = 6 cm and CD = 10 cm (applying the proved formula), its midline MN is:
mcqs.why: Using MN = (1/2)(AB + CD) = (1/2)(6 + 10) = (1/2)(16) = 8 cm, a direct application of the trapezium midline result proved in this lesson.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1 — The Perpendicular Bisector Theorem
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

The perpendicular bisector of a segment is the line that cuts the segment at its midpoint at a right angle. Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from the two ends of the segment, and every point equidistant from the two ends lies on the perpendicular bisector.

The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle meet at one point called the circumcentre. The circumcentre is equidistant from all three vertices, so it is the centre of the circle passing through the three vertices, called the circumcircle.

The Perpendicular Bisector Theorem

Figure in words: Triangle ABC is drawn. The perpendicular bisector of side AB and the perpendicular bisector of side AC are drawn and they meet at point O. Segments OA, OB and OC join O to the three vertices.

Step 1: Let the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC meet at O.

Step 2: O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB, so OA = OB.

Step 3: O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC, so OA = OC.

Step 4: Therefore OA = OB = OC.

Step 5: Hence O is equidistant from all three vertices A, B and C. This proves the theorem.

Worked Example 1 - Centre on the Perpendicular Bisector of a Chord

Figure in words: A circle has centre O and chord AB. Segment OM is drawn from O perpendicular to AB, meeting AB at M.

Step 1: In triangles OAM and OBM, OA = OB because both are radii of the same circle.

Step 2: OM is a common side, and angle OMA = angle OMB = 90 degrees because OM is perpendicular to AB.

Step 3: By RHS congruence, triangle OAM is congruent to triangle OBM.

Step 4: Therefore AM = MB, so OM bisects AB at a right angle.

Step 5: Hence OM is the perpendicular bisector of AB, and the centre O lies on the perpendicular bisector of the chord.

Worked Example 2 - Two Intersecting Circles

Figure in words: Two circles with centres O1 and O2 intersect at points A and B. The line O1O2 joining the centres crosses the common chord AB.

Step 1: O1A = O1B because both are radii of the first circle, so O1 is equidistant from A and B.

Step 2: O2A = O2B because both are radii of the second circle, so O2 is also equidistant from A and B.

Step 3: Every point equidistant from A and B lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

Step 4: Therefore both O1 and O2 lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, so the line O1O2 is the perpendicular bisector of AB.

Worked Example 3 - Mosque Equidistant from Three Markets

Step 1: Three markets A, B and C are not on a line, so they form a triangle.

Step 2: Draw the perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC and let them meet at the circumcentre.

Step 3: Build the mosque at that meeting point. By the perpendicular bisector property it is equidistant from A and B and also from A and C.

Step 4: Hence it is equidistant from all three markets A, B and C.

Remember

The centre of the circle through three non-collinear points is the circumcentre, the meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors of the segments joining them.

mcqs.q: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is:
options: Equidistant from the two ends of the segment
mcqs.why: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is equidistant from the two ends. This is the basic perpendicular bisector property used in Exercise 11.1.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC meet at O. Then:
mcqs.why: O is on the bisector of AB so OA = OB, and on the bisector of AC so OA = OC. Hence OA = OB = OC, so O is equidistant from all vertices.

mcqs.q: The centre of a circle lies on the perpendicular bisector of a chord because:
options: The radii to the chord ends are unequal
The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord
The chord passes through the centre
mcqs.why: Drop perpendicular OM to chord AB. Triangles OAM and OBM are congruent by RHS since OA = OB are radii, so AM = MB and OM is the perpendicular bisector.

mcqs.q: The centre of the circle through three non-collinear points is:
options: The circumcentre where perpendicular bisectors meet
mcqs.why: The circumcentre is equidistant from all three points, so a circle centred there passes through all three. It is where the perpendicular bisectors meet.

mcqs.q: Two circles intersect at A and B with centres O1 and O2. The line O1O2 is:
mcqs.why: O1A = O1B and O2A = O2B as radii, so both centres are equidistant from A and B and lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Hence O1O2 is that bisector.

mcqs.q: A mosque equidistant from three non-collinear markets A, B and C must be built at:
mcqs.why: The circumcentre is equidistant from A and B and from A and C by the perpendicular bisector property, so it is equidistant from all three markets.

mcqs.q: In the chord proof, triangles OAM and OBM are congruent by:
mcqs.why: OA = OB are radii, OM is common, and both angles at M are 90 degrees. Two right triangles with equal hypotenuse and a common side are congruent by RHS.

mcqs.q: Bisecting a side means dividing it into:
mcqs.why: Bisect means to divide into two equal parts. Review Exercise 11 states this as true: bisecting a side divides it into two equal parts.

mcqs.q: In an acute triangle, how many acute angles are there?
mcqs.why: An acute triangle has all three angles less than 90 degrees, so it has three acute angles. This is Review Exercise 11 Question 4(i), answer three.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of an acute triangle intersect:
mcqs.why: For an acute triangle the circumcentre lies inside, so the perpendicular bisectors intersect inside the triangle, as in Review Exercise 11 Question 4(iii).

lessons.title: Exercise 11.2 — Circumcentre and Perpendicular Bisectors
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

The circumcentre is the meeting point of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle. Its position depends on the angles: inside for an acute triangle, on the hypotenuse for a right triangle, and outside for an obtuse triangle. The altitudes of a triangle also meet at one point, called the orthocentre.

Theorem - Circumcentre of an Acute Triangle Lies Inside

Figure in words: Triangle ABC has all angles less than 90 degrees. The circumcentre O is shown inside the triangle, on the same side of BC as vertex A, and similarly for the other sides.

Step 1: For side BC, O lies on the same side of BC as A when angle A is less than 90 degrees.

Step 2: If angle A were 90 degrees, O would lie on BC, and if angle A were greater than 90 degrees, O would lie on the opposite side of BC from A.

Step 3: In an acute triangle all three angles are less than 90 degrees, so the same argument holds for every side.

Step 4: Therefore O lies inside the triangle, on the inner side of every side.

Worked Example 1 - Isosceles Trapezium

Figure in words: Isosceles trapezium ABCD has AB parallel to CD and AD = BC. A vertical axis of symmetry passes through the midpoints of AB and CD.

Step 1: The axis of symmetry is the perpendicular bisector of both AB and CD.

Step 2: By symmetry, the perpendicular bisectors of AD and BC meet this axis at the same point.

Step 3: Therefore the perpendicular bisectors of all four sides meet at one point, the circumcentre.

Worked Example 2 - Altitudes Meet at One Point

Figure in words: Triangle ABC is placed with A at (0, 0), B at (c, 0) on the x-axis, and C at (u, v) above the axis. The three altitudes are drawn from each vertex perpendicular to the opposite side.

Altitude from C: x = u

Altitude from B: y = (-u/v)(x - c)

Step 1: Place A at (0, 0), B at (c, 0) and C at (u, v).

Step 2: The altitude from C is vertical, so its equation is x = u.

Step 3: At x = u, the altitude from B gives y = u(c - u)/v.

Step 4: The altitude from A is y = (-(u - c)/v)x, and at x = u it also gives y = u(c - u)/v.

Step 5: All three altitudes pass through the same point (u, u(c - u)/v), so they meet at one point, the orthocentre.

Review Link - Equal Altitudes

If two altitudes of a triangle are equal, the triangle is isosceles, because area = (1/2) x base x altitude: equal altitudes with equal area force the corresponding sides to be equal.

Area of a triangle = (1/2) x base x altitude

mcqs.q: The circumcentre of an acute triangle lies:
