mcqs.why: All angles are acute, so for each side the circumcentre lies on the same side as the opposite vertex. Hence it lies inside the triangle.

mcqs.q: If angle A = 90 degrees, the circumcentre lies:
options: On BC, the side opposite A
mcqs.why: The source proof notes that if angle A = 90 degrees the circumcentre would lie on BC. For a right triangle it is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

mcqs.q: The altitudes of a triangle meet at:
mcqs.why: The three altitudes are concurrent at one point called the orthocentre. Exercise 11.2 Question 3 proves this with coordinates.

mcqs.q: In the coordinate proof, A, B and C are placed at:
mcqs.why: The proof places A at (0,0), B at (c,0) and C at (u,v). The altitude from C is then x = u, which makes the concurrency easy to check.

mcqs.q: The altitude from C in the coordinate proof is:
mcqs.why: C is at (u, v) and AB lies on the x-axis, so the altitude from C is vertical through x = u. Substituting x = u gives the common point.

mcqs.q: In an isosceles trapezium, the perpendicular bisectors of all four sides:
mcqs.why: The axis of symmetry is the perpendicular bisector of both parallel sides, and by symmetry the other two bisectors meet it at the same point, the circumcentre.

mcqs.q: If two altitudes of a triangle are equal, the triangle is:
mcqs.why: Area = (1/2) x base x altitude. With equal area and equal altitudes, the two corresponding sides must be equal, so the triangle is isosceles.

mcqs.q: The bisectors of the angles of a triangle are:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 11 states the angle bisectors are concurrent. They meet at the incentre, which is equidistant from all three sides.

mcqs.q: The incentre is equidistant from:
options: All three sides of the triangle
mcqs.why: A point on an angle bisector is equidistant from the sides of the angle. The incentre lies on all three bisectors, so it is equidistant from all three sides.

mcqs.q: For an obtuse angle A greater than 90 degrees, the circumcentre relative to BC lies:
options: On the opposite side of BC from A
On the same side as A
mcqs.why: The proof in Exercise 11.2 states: if angle A is greater than 90 degrees, O lies on the opposite side of BC from A, so for an obtuse triangle O is outside.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.3 — Angle Bisectors and Isosceles Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

An isosceles triangle has two equal sides and equal base angles. Points that are equidistant from the ends of the base lie on the perpendicular bisector of the base. The angle bisector theorem links an angle bisector to the opposite side: it divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides.

BD / DC = AB / AC (angle bisector theorem)

Worked Example 1 - Two Isosceles Triangles on a Common Base

Figure in words: Triangles ABC and DBC share the common base BC. A is above BC and D is below BC. AB = AC and DB = DC. Segment AD joins the two vertices and crosses BC at its midpoint at a right angle.

Step 1: AB = AC, so A is equidistant from B and C.

Step 2: DB = DC, so D is also equidistant from B and C.

Step 3: Both A and D therefore lie on the perpendicular bisector of BC.

Step 4: Hence the line AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC, so AD bisects BC at a right angle.

Worked Example 2 - Angle Bisectors That Bisect Opposite Sides

Figure in words: Triangle ABC has the bisector of angle A meeting BC at D, with BD = DC.

Step 1: The bisector of angle A meets BC at D and BD = DC is given.

Step 2: By the angle bisector theorem, BD/DC = AB/AC.

Step 3: Since BD = DC, BD/DC = 1, so AB/AC = 1 and AB = AC.

Step 4: Applying the same argument to the other bisectors gives all sides equal, so the triangle is isosceles, in fact equilateral in this full case.

Worked Example 3 - Equal Perpendiculars in an Isosceles Triangle

Figure in words: Isosceles triangle ABC has AB = AC, with A at the top. BD is perpendicular to AC and CE is perpendicular to AB.

Step 1: Draw BD perpendicular to AC and CE perpendicular to AB.

Step 2: In triangles BCE and CBD, angle BEC = angle CDB = 90 degrees.

Step 3: Angle EBC = angle DCB because they are the base angles of the isosceles triangle.

Step 4: BC is a common side, so by AAS the two triangles are congruent.

Step 5: Therefore CE = BD, so the perpendiculars from B and C to the opposite sides are equal.

Review Check

Triangles with equal sides also have equal angles, by SSS congruence. Each base angle of an isosceles obtuse triangle is not fixed at 45 degrees; for example a vertex angle of 100 degrees gives base angles of 40 degrees.

mcqs.q: Two isosceles triangles on common base BC with AB = AC and DB = DC: AD is:
mcqs.why: Both A and D are equidistant from B and C, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Hence AD bisects BC at a right angle.

mcqs.q: The angle bisector theorem states that the bisector of angle A divides BC so that:
mcqs.why: The bisector of angle A meeting BC at D gives BD/DC = AB/AC. If also BD = DC then AB = AC, proving the triangle is isosceles.

mcqs.q: In isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC, the perpendiculars from B and C to opposite sides are:
mcqs.why: Triangles BCE and CBD are congruent by AAS: right angles, equal base angles and common BC. Hence CE = BD, so the perpendiculars are equal.

mcqs.q: Triangles BCE and CBD in Example 3 are congruent by:
mcqs.why: They have a right angle each, equal base angles EBC and DCB, and common side BC. That is angle-angle-side, so AAS gives congruence and CE = BD.

mcqs.q: If the bisector of angle A also bisects BC, then:
mcqs.why: BD/DC = AB/AC by the bisector theorem and BD = DC, so AB/AC = 1 and AB = AC. The triangle is therefore isosceles at A.

mcqs.q: The base angles of an isosceles triangle are:
mcqs.why: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Their value is not fixed: vertex 100 degrees gives base angles of 40 degrees each.

mcqs.q: Triangles with equal sides also have equal angles. This statement is:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 11 marks this true. Equal sides give SSS congruence, and corresponding angles of congruent triangles are equal.

mcqs.q: Each base angle of an isosceles obtuse triangle is 45 degrees. This statement is:
options: True only if vertex is 100 degrees
False, it can be any value below 90 degrees
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 11 marks it false. The base angles can take any value less than 90 degrees, for example 40 degrees when the vertex angle is 100 degrees.

mcqs.q: A and D equidistant from B and C implies AD:
options: Bisects BC at a right angle
mcqs.why: Points equidistant from B and C lie on the perpendicular bisector of BC. Two such points A and D define that line, so AD bisects BC at a right angle.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC with AB = AC, angle EBC equals angle DCB because:
options: They are base angles of the isosceles triangle
mcqs.why: AB = AC makes BC the base, so the angles at B and C are the base angles and are equal. This equality is used in the AAS proof that CE = BD.

chapters.title: 12. Sides and Angles of a Triangle

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1 — Inequalities of the Sides and Angles of a Triangle
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

In any triangle, the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side, and the difference of any two sides is less than the third side. This is the triangle inequality.

The larger side lies opposite the larger angle, and the smaller side lies opposite the smaller angle. So to find the largest or smallest side, first find the largest or smallest angle using the angle sum 180 degrees.

The perpendicular distance from a point to a line is the shortest distance from that point to the line.

Worked Example 1 - Interior Point Inequality

Figure in words: Triangle ABC has an interior point O. Segments OA, OB and OC join O to the vertices, dividing the triangle into three smaller triangles OAB, OBC and OCA.

Step 1: In triangle OAB, OA + OB is greater than AB by the triangle inequality.

Step 2: In triangle OBC, OB + OC is greater than BC.

Step 3: In triangle OCA, OC + OA is greater than CA.

Step 4: Add the three inequalities: 2(OA + OB + OC) is greater than AB + BC + CA.

Step 5: Divide by 2 to get OA + OB + OC is greater than (1/2)(AB + BC + CA).

OA + OB + OC > (1/2)(AB + BC + CA)

Worked Example 2 - Largest Side

Step 1: In triangle ABC, angle B = 70 degrees and angle C = 45 degrees are given.

Step 2: Angle A = 180 - 70 - 45 = 65 degrees.

Step 3: The largest angle is angle B = 70 degrees.

Step 4: The side opposite angle B is AC, so AC is the largest side.

Worked Example 3 - Smallest Side

Step 1: In triangle ABC, angle A = 58 degrees and angle B = 65 degrees are given.

Step 2: Angle C = 180 - 58 - 65 = 57 degrees.

Step 3: The smallest angle is angle C = 57 degrees.

Step 4: The side opposite angle C is AB, so AB is the smallest side.

Worked Example 4 - Review: Angles 50 and 30 Degrees

Step 1: If angle A = 50 degrees and angle B = 30 degrees, then angle C = 180 - 50 - 30 = 100 degrees.

Step 2: Angle C is the largest angle, so the side opposite it, AB, is larger than the other two sides.

Useful Facts

A median is less than half the sum of the two adjacent sides, so a median in Review Exercise 12 is less than 9 cm. The diagonal of a rectangle is less than length + width, so with perimeter 22 cm the diagonal is less than 11 cm.

mcqs.q: The sum of any two sides of a triangle is:
options: Equal to half the third side
mcqs.why: The triangle inequality says the sum of two sides is greater than the third side. Review Exercise 12 marks this statement true.

mcqs.q: The difference of two sides of a triangle is:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 12 marks difference greater than third side as false. The difference of two sides is less than the third side.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC with B = 70 degrees and C = 45 degrees, the largest side is:
mcqs.why: Angle A = 180 - 70 - 45 = 65 degrees. The largest angle is B = 70 degrees, and the side opposite B is AC, so AC is largest.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC with A = 58 degrees and B = 65 degrees, the smallest side is:
mcqs.why: Angle C = 180 - 58 - 65 = 57 degrees, the smallest angle. The side opposite angle C is AB, so AB is the smallest side.

mcqs.q: For interior point O in triangle ABC, OA + OB + OC is:
mcqs.why: Adding OA+OB greater than AB, OB+OC greater than BC, OC+OA greater than CA gives 2(OA+OB+OC) greater than the perimeter, so the sum exceeds half the perimeter.

mcqs.q: The shortest distance from a point to a line is:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 12 marks this true: the perpendicular distance is the shortest distance from a point to a line, shorter than any oblique segment.

mcqs.q: If angle A = 50 degrees and angle B = 30 degrees in triangle ABC, the largest side is:
mcqs.why: Angle C = 180 - 50 - 30 = 100 degrees, the largest angle. The side opposite angle C is AB, so AB is larger than the other two sides.

mcqs.q: The largest angle of an obtuse triangle:
options: Can be any value between 90 and 180 degrees
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 12 marks largest angle is 100 degrees as false. An obtuse angle can take any value between 90 degrees and 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: The side opposite the obtuse angle in an obtuse triangle is:
mcqs.why: The obtuse angle is the largest angle, and the larger side lies opposite the larger angle. So the side opposite the obtuse angle is the largest side.

mcqs.q: If the perimeter of a rectangle is 22 cm, its diagonal is:
mcqs.why: Length + width = 11 cm and diagonal = sqrt(l^2 + w^2) which is less than l + w = 11 cm. So the diagonal is less than 11 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1 — Constructing a Triangle: Sides and Angles
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

A triangle can be constructed when two sides and the included angle are given (SAS), when one side and two angles are given (ASA), or when two sides and an angle opposite one side are given using an arc. Always draw one side first, construct the given angle at the correct vertex, then mark the second length or draw the arc.

Construction Steps - Two Equal Sides and Included Angle at Q

Finished figure in words: Triangle PQR has QR = 4.6 cm along the base, angle at Q is 35 degrees, and QP = 4.6 cm along the ray from Q, so PQ = QR. P is joined to R.

Step 1: Draw QR = 4.6 cm.

Step 2: At Q construct an angle of 35 degrees.

Step 3: Mark QP = 4.6 cm on the ray.

Step 4: Join PR. Triangle PQR is the required triangle.

Construction Steps - Isosceles Triangle with Vertex Angle 65 Degrees

Finished figure in words: Triangle ABC has AB = 5.1 cm, AC = 5.1 cm and angle A = 65 degrees between them. BC joins the two free ends.

Step 1: Draw AB = 5.1 cm.

Step 2: At A construct an angle of 65 degrees.

Step 3: Mark AC = 5.1 cm on the ray.

Step 4: Join BC. Triangle ABC is the required triangle.

Construction Steps - SAS with an Obtuse Angle

Finished figure in words: Triangle ABC has BC = 2.7 cm, angle B = 110 degrees (obtuse), and BA = 3.5 cm. AC joins the ends.

Step 1: Draw BC = 2.7 cm.

Step 2: At B construct an angle of 110 degrees.

Step 3: Mark BA = 3.5 cm on the ray.

Step 4: Join AC. Triangle ABC is the required triangle.

Construction Steps - One Side and Two Angles

Finished figure in words: Triangle DEF has DE = 5 cm, angle D = 45 degrees and angle E = 60 degrees. The rays from D and E meet at F.

Step 1: Draw DE = 5 cm.

Step 2: Construct an angle of 45 degrees at D and an angle of 60 degrees at E.

Step 3: The two rays meet at F. Triangle DEF is the required triangle.

Step 4: For BC = 5.8 cm with angle A = 30 degrees and angle B = 45 degrees, first find angle C = 180 - 30 - 45 = 105 degrees, draw BC, construct 45 degrees at B and 105 degrees at C, and the rays meet at A.

Construction Steps - Two Sides and Opposite Angle

Finished figure in words: Triangle ABC has BC = 4.1 cm, AC = 4.5 cm and angle B = 75 degrees opposite side AC.

Step 1: Construct angle B = 75 degrees and mark BC = 4.1 cm on one arm.

Step 2: With centre C and radius 4.5 cm draw an arc cutting the other arm at A.

Step 3: Join AC. Triangle ABC is the required triangle.

mcqs.q: To construct triangle PQR with angle Q = 35 degrees and PQ = QR = 4.6 cm, the first step is:
mcqs.why: The source steps draw QR = 4.6 cm first, then construct 35 degrees at Q, mark QP = 4.6 cm on the ray, and join PR to complete the triangle.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC with angle A = 65 degrees and AB = AC = 5.1 cm, after drawing AB you:
options: Construct 65 degrees at A and mark AC = 5.1 cm
mcqs.why: At A construct the 65 degree angle, mark AC = 5.1 cm on its ray, then join BC. The two equal sides meet at A with the included angle between them.

mcqs.q: Triangle LMN has angle M = 50 degrees, LM = 3.7 cm, MN = 2.5 cm. You draw MN first, then:
options: Construct 50 degrees at M and mark ML = 3.7 cm
mcqs.why: Draw MN = 2.5 cm, construct 50 degrees at M, mark ML = 3.7 cm on the ray, then join LN. The angle is at M between LM and MN.

mcqs.q: For triangle ABC with angle B = 110 degrees, AB = 3.5 cm, BC = 2.7 cm, the angle constructed at B is:
mcqs.why: The given angle at B is 110 degrees, which is obtuse. Draw BC = 2.7 cm, construct 110 degrees at B, mark BA = 3.5 cm, then join AC.

mcqs.q: Triangle XYZ has angle Z = 80 degrees, XY = 4.1 cm, YZ = 5 cm. The point X is found by:
options: An arc from Y with radius 4.1 cm cutting the ray from Z
mcqs.why: Draw YZ = 5 cm, construct 80 degrees at Z, then with centre Y and radius XY = 4.1 cm draw an arc cutting the other ray at X, and join XY.

mcqs.q: For DE = 5 cm, angle D = 45 degrees, angle E = 60 degrees, vertex F is:
options: Where the rays from D and E meet
Found by an arc from D only
mcqs.why: Draw DE = 5 cm and construct 45 degrees at D and 60 degrees at E. The two rays meet at F, giving triangle DEF by the ASA construction.

mcqs.q: For BC = 5.8 cm, angle A = 30 degrees, angle B = 45 degrees, angle C equals:
mcqs.why: Angle C = 180 - 30 - 45 = 105 degrees. Then draw BC, construct 45 degrees at B and 105 degrees at C, and the rays meet at A.

mcqs.q: For BC = 4.1 cm, AC = 4.5 cm, angle B = 75 degrees, A is found by:
options: An arc of 4.1 cm from B
An arc from C with radius 4.5 cm
mcqs.why: Construct angle B = 75 degrees, mark BC = 4.1 cm, then with centre C and radius AC = 4.5 cm draw an arc cutting the other arm at A, and join AC.

mcqs.q: The side opposite the largest angle of a triangle is:

lessons.title: Exercise 13.2 — Constructing Medians, Altitudes and Bisectors
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. An altitude is the perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side. An angle bisector halves an interior angle. The three medians meet at the centroid G, which divides each median in the ratio 2:1. The three altitudes meet at the orthocentre H. The three angle bisectors meet at the incentre I, equidistant from the sides. The three perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre O.

Centroid divides each median in the ratio 2 : 1

Construction Steps - Triangle from Three Sides, Then Bisectors

Finished figure in words: Triangle ABC has BC = 6 cm as base, CA = 4 cm and AB = 5 cm. The bisectors of angles A and B are drawn inside and meet at the incentre I.

Step 1: Draw BC = 6 cm.

Step 2: With centre B and radius 5 cm draw an arc, and with centre C and radius 4 cm draw an arc; the arcs meet at A.

Step 3: Join AB and AC to complete triangle ABC.

Step 4: Bisect angle A and bisect angle B; the two bisectors meet at the incentre I.

Construction Steps - Altitude from a Vertex

Finished figure in words: Triangle PQR has PQ = 5.7 cm, QR = 6.4 cm and PR = 4.4 cm. A perpendicular segment is drawn from Q down to side PR.

Step 1: Draw PR = 4.4 cm.

Step 2: Get Q from arcs of 5.7 cm from P and 6.4 cm from R, and join PQR.

Step 3: Draw the perpendicular from Q to PR. That perpendicular is the altitude from Q.

Construction Steps - Perpendicular Bisectors in a Right Triangle

Finished figure in words: Triangle TUV has TU = 7 cm, angle T = 60 degrees and angle U = 30 degrees, so angle V = 90 degrees. The perpendicular bisectors of the three sides meet at O, the midpoint of hypotenuse TU.

Step 1: Draw TU = 7 cm.

Step 2: Construct 60 degrees at T and 30 degrees at U; the rays meet at V.

Step 3: Bisect the three sides and draw the perpendicular bisector of each side.

Step 4: All three perpendicular bisectors meet at the same point O, the circumcentre, which is the midpoint of the hypotenuse TU.

Construction Steps - Altitudes of Triangle KLM

Finished figure in words: Triangle KLM has KL = 4.8 cm, LM = 5.2 cm and MK = 4.5 cm. Three altitudes are drawn, one from each vertex perpendicular to the opposite side, meeting at one point.

Step 1: Draw KL = 4.8 cm.

Step 2: Get M from arcs of 5.2 cm from L and 4.5 cm from K, and join KLM.

Step 3: Draw the altitude from each vertex to the opposite side.

Step 4: Verify that all three altitudes meet at one point, the orthocentre.

Definitions from Review

A segment joining a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side is an altitude. A segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side is a median. The perpendicular bisectors of the sides are concurrent.

mcqs.q: The three medians of a triangle meet at:
mcqs.why: Medians join vertices to opposite midpoints and are concurrent at the centroid G, which divides each median in the ratio 2:1.

mcqs.q: The centroid divides each median in the ratio:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 13 confirms the medians cut each other in the ratio 2:1. The longer part is from the vertex to the centroid.

mcqs.q: The three altitudes of a triangle meet at:
mcqs.why: Altitudes are perpendiculars from vertices to opposite sides. They are concurrent at the orthocentre, as shown in Exercises 11.2 and 13.2.

mcqs.q: The three angle bisectors meet at the incentre, which is:
mcqs.why: Bisecting the three interior angles gives bisectors meeting at I, the incentre, which is equidistant from all three sides of the triangle.

mcqs.q: A line segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side is a:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 13 defines this exactly: vertex to midpoint of opposite side is a median. An altitude must also be perpendicular, which a median need not be.

mcqs.q: A line segment from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side is an:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 13 defines the altitude as the segment joining a vertex and perpendicular to the opposite side. Medians go to midpoints instead.

mcqs.why: Angle V = 180 - 60 - 30 = 90 degrees, so the triangle is right-angled at V and the circumcentre is the midpoint of hypotenuse TU.

mcqs.q: For triangle ABC with BC = 6 cm, CA = 4 cm, AB = 5 cm, point A is found by:
options: Arcs of 6 cm from both ends
An arc of 4 cm from B only
Arcs of 5 cm from B and 4 cm from C
mcqs.why: Draw BC = 6 cm, then A is the meeting of an arc of radius AB = 5 cm from B and an arc of radius CA = 4 cm from C. Then join ABC.

mcqs.why: Review Exercise 13: if all three medians are equal the triangle is equilateral. Equal medians force the sides to be equal.

mcqs.why: Review Exercise 13 states the three altitudes of an equilateral triangle are equal to each other, by the symmetry of equal sides and angles.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.3 — Figures of Equal Area
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

Figures of equal area can have different shapes and different perimeters. A square can be built with area equal to a given rectangle by using the mean proportional of the rectangle's two sides. A triangle can be converted into a rectangle of equal area by keeping the same base and halving the altitude.

Area of rectangle = length x width

Area of triangle = (1/2) x base x altitude

Side of equal-area square = sqrt(area of rectangle)

Construction Steps - Square Equal in Area to a Rectangle

Finished figure in words: A rectangle is drawn. One side is extended by the length of the other side, a semicircle is drawn on the whole extended line, and a perpendicular at the junction meets the semicircle. That perpendicular becomes the side of the required square.

Step 1: Draw the given rectangle.

Step 2: Extend one side of the rectangle by the length of the other side.

Step 3: Bisect the extended line and draw a semicircle on it as diameter.

Step 4: Erect a perpendicular at the end of the first side, meeting the semicircle.

Step 5: That perpendicular is the mean proportional of the two sides and is the side of the required square. Construct the square on it. Its area equals the area of the rectangle.

Worked Example 1 - Rectangle 4.5 cm by 2.2 cm

Step 1: Area of rectangle = 4.5 x 2.2 = 9.9 square cm.

Area = 4.5 x 2.2 = 9.9 cm^2

Step 2: Side of the equal-area square = sqrt(9.9) which is about 3.15 cm, and its area is also 9.9 square cm.

Side = sqrt(9.9) = 3.15 cm (approx.)

Step 3: Perimeter of square = 4 x 3.15 = 12.6 cm.

Step 4: Perimeter of rectangle = 2(4.5 + 2.2) = 13.4 cm.

Step 5: Since 12.6 is less than 13.4, the perimeter of the square is less than the perimeter of the rectangle, although the areas are equal.

Worked Example 2 - Triangle to Rectangle of Equal Area

Finished figure in words: A triangle with base 4 cm and other sides 3.6 cm and 3.8 cm is drawn. Its altitude h is about 3.11 cm. A rectangle with the same base 4 cm and height h/2, about 1.55 cm, is built beside it.

Step 1: Construct the triangle with base 4 cm and arcs of 3.6 cm and 3.8 cm for the other sides.

Step 2: Draw the altitude from the vertex to the base; h is about 3.11 cm and the area is about 6.22 square cm.

Step 3: Bisect the altitude and draw a line through its midpoint parallel to the base.

Step 4: Complete the rectangle with base 4 cm and height h/2, about 1.55 cm.

Step 5: Area of rectangle = 4 x 1.55 = about 6.22 square cm, equal to the area of the triangle.

Worked Example 3 - Base 6 cm Triangle

Step 1: Construct the triangle with base 6 cm and other sides 5 cm and 6 cm.

Step 2: Its altitude h is about 4.55 cm and its area is about 13.64 square cm.

Step 3: Build the rectangle with base 6 cm and height h/2, about 2.27 cm.

Step 4: Area of rectangle = 6 x 2.27 = about 13.64 square cm, equal to the triangle.

mcqs.q: The side of a square equal in area to a rectangle is:
options: The mean proportional of the rectangle's two sides
The sum of the two sides
mcqs.why: The construction gives the perpendicular to the semicircle, which is the mean proportional of the two sides. The square on it has area equal to the rectangle.

mcqs.q: Area of a rectangle 4.5 cm by 2.2 cm is:
mcqs.why: Area = length x width = 4.5 x 2.2 = 9.9 square cm. The equal-area square has the same area, 9.9 square cm.

mcqs.why: Side = sqrt(9.9) which is about 3.15 cm, because 3.15 x 3.15 is about 9.9. This is the value measured in Exercise 13.3 Question 2.

options: Square perimeter is less than rectangle perimeter
mcqs.why: Perimeter of square = 4 x 3.15 = 12.6 cm and of rectangle = 2(4.5+2.2) = 13.4 cm. Since 12.6 is less than 13.4, the square perimeter is less.

mcqs.q: To convert a triangle into an equal-area rectangle with the same base, the rectangle height is:
mcqs.why: Area of triangle = (1/2) x base x h. With the same base, a rectangle needs height h/2 so base x (h/2) equals the triangle area.

mcqs.q: For the triangle with base 4 cm, altitude about 3.11 cm, the equal-area rectangle height is about:
mcqs.why: Halve the altitude: 3.11 / 2 is about 1.55 cm. Rectangle area = 4 x 1.55 = about 6.22 square cm, equal to the triangle area.

mcqs.q: A quadrilateral with every angle 90 degrees and all sides equal is a:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 13: all angles 90 degrees with all sides equal defines a square. A rectangle need not have equal sides.

mcqs.q: The diagonals of a rectangle are:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 13 states the diagonals of a rectangle are equal to each other. They also bisect each other, unlike the options given.

mcqs.q: If each base angle of an isosceles triangle is 45 degrees, the vertex angle is:
mcqs.why: Vertex angle = 180 - 45 - 45 = 90 degrees. This is Review Exercise 13 Question 2(vii), answer 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: If two sides of a triangle are equal, the triangle will be:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 13: if two sides of a triangle are equal, the triangle is isosceles. Equilateral requires all three sides equal.

lessons.title: Exercise 14.1 — Areas and Parallelograms
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

The area of a parallelogram equals base times altitude, where altitude is the perpendicular distance between the parallels containing the base and the opposite side.

Area of a parallelogram = base x altitude

Parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels have equal areas. Two triangles with the same base and equal altitudes have equal areas. Equal area does not mean congruent: figures can have equal areas but different shapes.

Theorem - Parallelogram and Rectangle on the Same Base

Figure in words: Parallelogram ABCD and rectangle EFCD share the same base DC. Both lie between the same parallels EB and DC. AL is drawn perpendicular to DC.

Step 1: Parallelogram ABCD and rectangle EFCD are on the same base DC and between the same parallels EB and DC, so their areas are equal.

Step 2: Area of the rectangle = DC x FC.

Step 3: FC = AL because both are perpendicular distances between the same parallels.

Step 4: Therefore area of ABCD = DC x AL, that is, base times altitude.

Worked Example 1 - Median Divides a Triangle into Equal Areas

Figure in words: Triangle ABC has median AD, where D is the midpoint of BC. The two triangles ABD and ACD share the same altitude from A.

Step 1: A median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side, so BD = DC; the two triangles have equal bases.

Step 2: Both triangles have the same altitude from A to BC.

Step 3: Triangles with equal bases and the same altitude have equal areas.

Step 4: Hence the median divides the triangle into two triangles of equal area.

Worked Example 2 - Rhombus Diagonals Give Four Equal Areas

Step 1: The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other.

Step 2: Each of the four triangles has base equal to a half-diagonal and altitude equal to the other half-diagonal.

Step 3: Equal bases with equal altitudes give equal areas, so all four triangles have equal areas.

Worked Example 3 - Equal-Area Parallelograms with the Same Base

Step 1: Area of a parallelogram = base x altitude.

Step 2: Two parallelograms have equal areas and the same base.

Step 3: Since base x altitude is the same and the base is the same, their altitudes must also be equal.

Worked Example 4 - Angle Bisector in an Equilateral Triangle

Step 1: In an equilateral triangle the angle bisector is also the median to the opposite side.

Step 2: It therefore bisects the opposite side, giving two triangles with equal bases and the same altitude.

Step 3: Hence the bisector divides the equilateral triangle into two triangles of equal area.

Note on a Defective Item

Exercise 14.1 Question 3 as printed gives BC = 7 cm and AC = 11 cm but no height, so the area cannot be determined from those data alone. It is excluded from the MCQs.

mcqs.q: Area of a parallelogram equals:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 14 confirms area of a parallelogram = base x altitude. For ABCD on base DC with altitude AL, area = DC x AL.

mcqs.q: Parallelogram ABCD and rectangle EFCD on same base DC between same parallels have:
options: Zero area difference only if square
mcqs.why: Same base and between the same parallels means the same altitude, so base x altitude is the same. Hence their areas are equal.

mcqs.q: A median of a triangle divides it into two triangles of:
mcqs.why: The two triangles have equal bases (the median reaches the midpoint) and the same altitude from the vertex, so their areas are equal.

mcqs.q: Two equal-area parallelograms with the same base must have:
mcqs.why: Area = base x altitude. Equal areas with the same base force base x altitude to match, so the altitudes are also equal.

mcqs.q: A rhombus is divided by its diagonals into four triangles of:
mcqs.why: The diagonals bisect each other, so the four triangles have equal bases (half-diagonals) and equal altitudes, giving four equal areas.

options: Not necessary - equal area does not guarantee congruence
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 14: equal-area triangles are not necessarily congruent. Different base-altitude pairs can give the same area with different shapes.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side is called the:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 14 defines this as the altitude. The median joins the vertex to the midpoint, which is a different segment.

mcqs.q: Parallelograms with the same base and same altitude are:
mcqs.why: Same base and same altitude give the same base x altitude value, so they are equal in area, though they need not be congruent in shape.

mcqs.q: The diagonal of a rectangle divides it into:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 14 marks this true: a rectangle diagonal creates two congruent right triangles, each half the rectangle area.

mcqs.q: The statement a median is the perpendicular from a vertex is:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 14 marks it false. The perpendicular from a vertex is the altitude; the median joins the vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

chapters.title: 15. Projection of a Side of a Triangle

lessons.title: Exercise 15.1 — Obtuse-Angled Triangles and Projection
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

The projection of a side of a triangle is its shadow segment on another side or its extension. For an obtuse triangle the square on the side opposite the obtuse angle is greater than the sum of the squares on the other two sides, by twice the product of one side and the projection of the other on it.

(mAB)^2 = (mAC)^2 + (mBC)^2 + 2(mAC)(mCD) (obtuse at C)

For a right triangle this reduces to Pythagoras: the extra term vanishes.

(mAC)^2 = (mAB)^2 + (mBC)^2 (right-angled at B)

Figure and Worked Example - Finding AB with Obtuse Angle 120 Degrees

Figure in words: Triangle ABC has angle C = 120 degrees, obtuse, with AC = 3 cm and BC = 6 cm. Side AC is extended beyond C to point D, and BD is drawn perpendicular to the extension, so CD is the projection segment outside the triangle.

Step 1: Let D be the foot of the perpendicular from B to AC extended.

Step 2: CD = BC cos(180 - angle C) = 6 x cos(60 degrees).

CD = 6 x cos 60 = 6 x 0.5 = 3 cm

Step 3: By the obtuse-angle theorem, (AB)^2 = (AC)^2 + (BC)^2 + 2(AC)(CD).

(mAB)^2 = 9 + 36 + 2 x 3 x 3 = 63

Step 4: Therefore AB = sqrt(63), which is about 7.94 cm.

mAB = sqrt(63) = 7.94 cm (approx.)

Review Form

In obtuse triangle ABC the review form writes the missing term as 2(AB)(AD), where AD is the projection of AC on AB extended. The pattern is always: square on the side opposite the obtuse angle = sum of squares on the other sides + twice the product term.

mcqs.q: In the obtuse theorem, D is:
options: The foot of the perpendicular from B to AC extended
mcqs.why: D is defined as the foot of the perpendicular from B onto AC extended. CD is then the projection segment used in the obtuse-angle formula.

mcqs.q: With BC = 6 cm and angle C = 120 degrees, CD equals:
mcqs.why: CD = BC cos(180 - 120) = 6 x cos 60 = 6 x 0.5 = 3 cm. The cosine of 60 degrees is one half, halving the 6 cm side.

mcqs.q: With AC = 3 cm, BC = 6 cm, CD = 3 cm, (AB)^2 equals:
mcqs.why: (AB)^2 = (AC)^2 + (BC)^2 + 2(AC)(CD) = 9 + 36 + 18 = 63. The plus term appears because angle C is obtuse.

mcqs.q: AB in that triangle is:
mcqs.why: (AB)^2 = 63, so AB = sqrt(63) which is approximately 7.94 cm. It is not a whole number, so the exact form sqrt(63) is kept.

mcqs.q: For an obtuse angle, the formula uses:
mcqs.why: The obtuse-angle theorem adds the term: square = sum of squares + 2(side)(projection). The acute theorem subtracts the corresponding term instead.

mcqs.q: Review Exercise 15: in obtuse triangle ABC, (BC)^2 = (AC)^2 + (AB)^2 + blank. The blank is:
mcqs.why: The review answer is 2(AB)(AD) where AD is the projection of AC on AB extended. This matches the obtuse theorem pattern with the plus sign.

mcqs.q: If angle B = 90 degrees in triangle ABC, then (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 equals:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 15 gives (AC)^2. With a right angle the projection term vanishes and Pythagoras gives (AB)^2 + (BC)^2 = (AC)^2.

mcqs.q: Sides 8 cm, 15 cm and 17 cm form:
mcqs.why: 8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2, so Pythagoras holds exactly. Review Exercise 15 classifies 8, 15, 17 as a right triangle.

mcqs.q: A triangle with all sides 4 cm is called:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 15: every side equal to 4 cm means all three sides are equal, which is an equilateral triangle.

mcqs.q: cos(60 degrees) used in finding CD equals:
mcqs.why: CD = 6 x cos 60 and the source uses cos 60 = 0.5 to get CD = 3 cm. This value drives the whole AB calculation in Exercise 15.1.

lessons.title: Exercise 15.2 — Acute-Angled Triangles and Identifying Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

For an acute triangle the square on a side is less than the sum of the squares on the other two sides, by twice the product of one side and the projection of the other on it.

(mBC)^2 = (mAB)^2 + (mAC)^2 - 2(mAB)(projection) (acute angle)

To classify a triangle from its sides, compare the square of the largest side with the sum of the squares of the other two: equal means right-angled, less means acute, greater means obtuse.

Worked Example 1 - Acute Theorem with Angle A = 30 Degrees

Figure in words: Triangle ABC has acute angle A = 30 degrees. The projection of AC on AB is segment AD, where D is the foot of the perpendicular from C onto AB.

Step 1: By the acute-angle theorem, (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(AD), where AD is the projection of AC on AB.

Step 2: AD = (AC) cos 30 degrees = (AC)(sqrt(3)/2).

AD = (mAC) x (sqrt(3)/2)

Step 3: Substitute: (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(AC)(sqrt(3)/2).

Step 4: Simplify to (BC)^2 = (AC)^2 + (AB)^2 - sqrt(3)(AB)(AC), which is the required result.

(mBC)^2 = (mAC)^2 + (mAB)^2 - sqrt(3)(mAB)(mAC)

Worked Example 2 - Sides 3, 4, 5

Step 1: The largest side is 5, and 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25.

Step 2: 5^2 = 25, which equals 25.

Step 3: Since the square of the largest side equals the sum of the other squares, the triangle is right-angled.

Worked Example 3 - Sides 4, 7, 8

Step 1: The largest side is 8, and 4^2 + 7^2 = 16 + 49 = 65.

Step 2: 8^2 = 64, and 65 is greater than 64.

Step 3: Since the sum of the squares exceeds the square of the largest side, the triangle is acute-angled.

Note on a Defective Item

Exercise 15.2 Question 2 as printed leaves the value of BC blank, so that triangle cannot be solved. It is excluded from the MCQs.

mcqs.q: For an acute angle, the projection formula uses:
mcqs.why: The acute-angle theorem subtracts: (BC)^2 = (AB)^2 + (AC)^2 - 2(AB)(AD). The obtuse theorem adds the term instead.

mcqs.q: With angle A = 30 degrees, the projection AD of AC on AB is:
mcqs.why: AD = (AC) cos 30 and cos 30 = sqrt(3)/2, so AD = (AC)(sqrt(3)/2). Substituting gives the sqrt(3)(AB)(AC) term.

mcqs.q: The proved result for angle A = 30 degrees is (BC)^2 equals:
mcqs.why: Substituting AD = (AC)(sqrt(3)/2) into the acute theorem, 2 x sqrt(3)/2 = sqrt(3), giving (BC)^2 = (AC)^2 + (AB)^2 - sqrt(3)(AB)(AC).

mcqs.q: Sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm form:
mcqs.why: 3^2 + 4^2 = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5^2. Equality in Pythagoras means the triangle is right-angled, as in Exercise 15.2 Question 3.

mcqs.q: Sides 4 cm, 7 cm, 8 cm form:
mcqs.why: Largest side 8: 4^2 + 7^2 = 65 which is greater than 8^2 = 64, so the angle opposite 8 is acute and the triangle is acute-angled.

mcqs.q: To classify a triangle, you compare the square of the largest side with:
options: The sum of squares of the other two sides
mcqs.why: Equal means right, less means acute, greater means obtuse. This comparison is exactly how Questions 3 and 4 of Exercise 15.2 are solved.

mcqs.q: If the square of the largest side is greater than the sum of the other squares, the triangle is:
mcqs.why: A larger square than the sum means the opposite angle exceeds 90 degrees by the projection theorems, so the triangle is obtuse.

mcqs.q: cos(30 degrees) in the acute proof equals:
mcqs.why: The proof uses AD = (AC) cos 30 = (AC)(sqrt(3)/2). Hence cos 30 degrees is sqrt(3)/2 in this derivation.

mcqs.q: Sides 8, 15, 17 satisfy 64 + 225 = 289, so they form:
mcqs.why: 64 + 225 = 289 = 17^2, so Pythagoras holds and the triangle is right-angled. This is also Review Exercise 15 Question 1(iv).

mcqs.q: In the acute theorem, AD represents:
options: The projection of AC on AB
mcqs.why: AD is the projection of AC on AB: the foot D of the perpendicular from C splits AB, and AD is the shadow of AC along AB.

chapters.title: 16. Introduction to Coordinate Geometry / Analytical Geometry

lessons.title: Exercise 16.1 — The Distance Formula
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

The distance between two points is found with the distance formula, which comes from Pythagoras in the coordinate plane.

|AB| = sqrt((x2 - x1)^2 + (y2 - y1)^2)

For points A(a, 0) on the x-axis and B(0, b) on the y-axis, the formula simplifies because the differences are a and b.

AB = sqrt(a^2 + b^2)

Worked Example 1 - Distance Between (6, 6) and (-4, 5)

Step 1: Write x2 - x1 = -4 - 6 = -10 and y2 - y1 = 5 - 6 = -1.

Step 2: Square them: 100 and 1.

Step 3: Add and take the square root: d = sqrt(100 + 1) = sqrt(101) units.

d = sqrt((-4 - 6)^2 + (5 - 6)^2) = sqrt(101)

Worked Example 2 - Distance Between (2, 3) and (0, 1)

Step 1: Differences are 0 - 2 = -2 and 1 - 3 = -2.

Step 2: d = sqrt(4 + 4) = sqrt(8) = 2 sqrt(2) units.

d = sqrt((0 - 2)^2 + (1 - 3)^2) = 2sqrt(2)

Step 3: Note the vertical pair (2, 3) and (2, 2) gives d = sqrt(0 + 1) = 1 unit, showing equal x-coordinates leave only the y-difference.

Worked Example 3 - Points on the Axes

Step 1: For A(a, 0) and B(0, b), AB = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).

Step 2: With a = -3, b = -4: AB = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 units.

Step 3: With a = -9, b = 6: AB = sqrt(81 + 36) = sqrt(117) = 3 sqrt(13) units.

Step 4: With a = sqrt(2), b = -2 sqrt(2): AB = sqrt(2 + 8) = sqrt(10) units.

Worked Example 4 - Perimeter of a Triangle

Figure in words: Points A(0, 0), B(4, 0) and C(2, 2 sqrt(3)) are plotted; C sits above the midpoint of AB, forming an equilateral triangle.

Step 1: AB = 4 units along the x-axis.

Step 2: BC = sqrt((2 - 4)^2 + (2 sqrt(3))^2) = sqrt(4 + 12) = 4 units.

Step 3: CA = sqrt(2^2 + (2 sqrt(3))^2) = sqrt(4 + 12) = 4 units.

Step 4: Perimeter = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 units, and the triangle is equilateral.

Review Facts

The distance of (6, 0) from the origin is 6 units, not 36. In the fourth quadrant x is positive and y is negative. The x-axis and y-axis intersect at (0, 0).

mcqs.q: The distance formula for A(x1,y1) and B(x2,y2) is:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 16 gives |AB| = sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2). It is Pythagoras applied to the coordinate differences.

mcqs.q: Distance between (6,6) and (-4,5) is:
mcqs.why: d = sqrt((-4-6)^2 + (5-6)^2) = sqrt(100+1) = sqrt(101) units. Both differences must be squared before adding.

mcqs.q: Distance between (2,3) and (2,2) is:
mcqs.why: d = sqrt((2-2)^2 + (2-3)^2) = sqrt(0+1) = 1 unit. Equal x-coordinates mean the distance is just the y-difference.

mcqs.q: Distance between (2,3) and (0,1) is:
mcqs.why: d = sqrt((0-2)^2 + (1-3)^2) = sqrt(4+4) = sqrt(8) = 2sqrt(2) units, as computed in Exercise 16.1 Question 1(iii).

mcqs.q: For A(a,0) with a = -3 and B(0,b) with b = -4, AB equals:
mcqs.why: AB = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) = sqrt(9+16) = sqrt(25) = 5 units. Signs disappear because each coordinate is squared.

mcqs.q: For a = -9, b = 6, the distance AB equals:
mcqs.why: AB = sqrt(81 + 36) = sqrt(117) = 3sqrt(13) units, since 117 = 9 x 13 and sqrt(9) = 3 comes out of the root.

mcqs.q: For a = sqrt(2), b = -2sqrt(2), AB equals:
mcqs.why: AB = sqrt(2 + 8) = sqrt(10) units because (sqrt(2))^2 = 2 and (2sqrt(2))^2 = 8. The negative sign vanishes on squaring.

mcqs.q: Perimeter of triangle A(0,0), B(4,0), C(2,2sqrt(3)) is:
mcqs.why: Each side is 4: AB = 4, BC = sqrt(4+12) = 4, CA = 4. Perimeter = 4+4+4 = 12 units and the triangle is equilateral.

mcqs.q: Distance of point (6,0) from the origin is:
mcqs.why: Distance = sqrt(6^2 + 0^2) = 6 units. Review Exercise 16 marks 36 units false; 36 is 6 squared, before taking the root.

mcqs.q: In the fourth quadrant:
options: x is positive and y is negative
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 16: in the fourth quadrant x is greater than 0 and y is less than 0. First quadrant has both positive, third has both negative.

lessons.title: Exercise 16.2 — Collinear Points and Types of Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

Three points are collinear if they lie on the same line. Using distances, they are collinear when the largest distance equals the sum of the other two. Non-collinear points form a triangle: all sides equal means equilateral, two sides equal means isosceles, all sides different means scalene. Pythagoras on the side lengths tells whether the triangle is right-angled.

Collinear test: largest distance = sum of the other two distances

Worked Example 1 - Collinear Points P, Q, R

Step 1: P(-3, -4), Q(2, 6): PQ = sqrt(25 + 100) = sqrt(125) = 5 sqrt(5).

Step 2: Q(2, 6), R(0, 2): QR = sqrt(4 + 16) = sqrt(20) = 2 sqrt(5).

Step 3: P(-3, -4), R(0, 2): PR = sqrt(9 + 36) = sqrt(45) = 3 sqrt(5).

Step 4: PR + QR = 3 sqrt(5) + 2 sqrt(5) = 5 sqrt(5) = PQ, so the points are collinear, with R between P and Q.

Worked Example 2 - Equilateral Triangle

Step 1: L(0, sqrt(3)), M(-1, 0): LM = sqrt(1 + 3) = 2.

Step 2: M(-1, 0), N(1, 0): MN = 2.

Step 3: N(1, 0), L(0, sqrt(3)): NL = sqrt(1 + 3) = 2.

Step 4: All three sides equal 2, so LMN is an equilateral triangle. Similarly A(-1, 0), B(1, 0), C(0, sqrt(3)) all give sides 2 and are non-collinear.

Worked Example 3 - Isosceles Right Triangle

Step 1: A(2, 3), B(8, 11): AB = sqrt(36 + 64) = 10.

Step 2: B(8, 11), C(0, 17): BC = sqrt(64 + 36) = 10.

Step 3: A(2, 3), C(0, 17): AC = sqrt(4 + 196) = sqrt(200) = 10 sqrt(2).

Step 4: AB = BC, so the triangle is isosceles, and AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2, so it is also right-angled.

Worked Example 4 - Scalene and Quadrilaterals

Step 1: P(1, 2), Q(3, 4), R(0, -1) give PQ = 2 sqrt(2), QR = sqrt(34), RP = sqrt(10): all different, so the triangle is scalene.

Step 2: A(3, 2), B(4, 1), C(5, 4), D(6, 3) give opposite sides sqrt(2) and sqrt(10) with equal diagonals 2 sqrt(2), so ABCD is a rectangle.

Step 3: For equilateral A(3, 1), B(9, 1), C(6, k): AB = 6 and AC = 6 gives (k - 1)^2 = 27, so k = 1 plus or minus 3 sqrt(3).

k = 1 +/- 3sqrt(3)

Notes on Defective Items

Exercise 16.2 Question 9 prints D(0, 3) duplicating B(0, 3); read as D(0, -3) the points form a rhombus, not a square, since diagonals 4 and 6 differ. Question 11 claims OABC is not a parallelogram, but the distances and midpoints show it IS a parallelogram. Both are excluded as printed and noted here only as cautions.

mcqs.q: Points P(-3,-4), Q(2,6), R(0,2) are collinear because:
mcqs.why: PQ = 5sqrt(5), PR = 3sqrt(5), QR = 2sqrt(5) and 3sqrt(5)+2sqrt(5) = 5sqrt(5) = PQ. Largest equals sum of other two, so they are collinear.

mcqs.q: Points A(-1,0), B(1,0), C(0,sqrt(3)) are non-collinear because:
options: No sum of two distances equals the third
mcqs.why: AB = BC = AC = 2, and 2+2 is not equal to 2, so no largest distance equals the sum of the others. They form an equilateral triangle instead.
LM = sqrt(1+3) = 2, MN = 2, NL = 2. All three sides are equal, which defines an equilateral triangle.

mcqs.q: A(2,3), B(8,11), C(0,17) with AB = BC = 10, AC = 10sqrt(2) form:
mcqs.why: AB = BC = 10 gives two equal sides, so isosceles. Also AB^2+BC^2 = 200 = AC^2, so it is right-angled at B as well.

mcqs.q: A(-1,2), B(7,5), C(2,-6) with AB = AC = sqrt(73), BC = sqrt(146): the triangle is:
mcqs.why: AB^2 + AC^2 = 73+73 = 146 = BC^2, so Pythagoras holds and it is right-angled. The source answer is No, it is not obtuse.

mcqs.q: For equilateral A(3,1), B(9,1), C(6,k), k equals:
mcqs.why: AB = 6, so AC = 6 gives 9 + (k-1)^2 = 36, (k-1)^2 = 27, hence k = 1 +/- 3sqrt(3). Both signs give valid positions for C.

mcqs.q: P(1,2), Q(3,4), R(0,-1) form a scalene triangle because:
mcqs.why: PQ = 2sqrt(2), QR = sqrt(34), RP = sqrt(10): all three lengths differ, which is the definition of a scalene triangle.

mcqs.q: A(3,2), B(4,1), C(5,4), D(6,3) form a rectangle because:
options: Opposite sides equal and diagonals equal
mcqs.why: AB = CD = sqrt(2), BC = DA = sqrt(10) (a parallelogram) and diagonals AC = BD = 2sqrt(2) are equal, which makes it a rectangle.

mcqs.q: Three points are collinear when (B between A and C):
options: AB = BC + AC in distance terms mAB = mBC + mAC
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 16 gives mAB = mBC + mAC when B lies between A and C. Collinear points lie on the same line and cannot form a triangle.

mcqs.q: All sides of a scalene triangle are equal. This statement is:
options: False - no two sides are equal
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 16 marks it false. In a scalene triangle no two sides are equal; equal sides would make it isosceles or equilateral.

lessons.title: Exercise 16.3 — The Mid-Point Formula
lessons.notes_html:
Key Ideas

The midpoint of a segment is the average of the endpoints coordinates. The centre of a circle is the midpoint of any diameter.

Midpoint = ((x1 + x2)/2, (y1 + y2)/2)

Worked Example 1 - Midpoints of Pairs

Step 1: B(4, 8) and A(2, 6): midpoint = ((4 + 2)/2, (8 + 6)/2) = (3, 7).

Step 2: P(-3, -1) and Q(5, 2): midpoint = ((-3 + 5)/2, (-1 + 2)/2) = (1, 1/2).

Step 3: L(0, 6) and M(-8, 0): midpoint = ((0 - 8)/2, (6 + 0)/2) = (-4, 3).

Step 4: C(0, 0) and D(2 sqrt(3), 4 sqrt(3)): midpoint = (sqrt(3), 2 sqrt(3)).

Worked Example 2 - Centre and Other End of a Diameter

Step 1: Endpoints A(-5, 6) and B(3, -4): centre = ((-5 + 3)/2, (6 - 4)/2) = (-1, 1).

Step 2: Centre (3, 4) with one endpoint (4, 6): let the other endpoint be (x, y). Then (4 + x)/2 = 3 gives x = 2, and (6 + y)/2 = 4 gives y = 2.

Step 3: The other endpoint is (2, 2).

Worked Example 3 - Centre and Radius

Step 1: Endpoints A(-3, 4) and B(11, 6): centre = ((-3 + 11)/2, (4 + 6)/2) = (4, 5).

Step 2: Diameter = sqrt((11 + 3)^2 + (6 - 4)^2) = sqrt(200) = 10 sqrt(2).

Step 3: Radius = half the diameter = 5 sqrt(2) units.

Radius = (10sqrt(2))/2 = 5sqrt(2)

Proof 1 - Diagonals of a Parallelogram Bisect Each Other

Figure in words: Parallelogram OABC is placed with O(0, 0), A(a, 0), C(b, d) and B(a + b, d). The diagonals are OB and AC.

Step 1: Midpoint of diagonal OB = ((a + b)/2, d/2).

Step 2: Midpoint of diagonal AC = ((a + b)/2, d/2).

Step 3: Both midpoints are the same point, so the diagonals bisect each other.

Proof 2 - Equal Medians Imply Isosceles

Step 1: Let equal medians AD and BE meet at centroid G, with AG = (2/3)AD = (2/3)BE = BG, so triangle AGB is isosceles and angle BAG = angle ABG.

Step 2: In triangles ABD and BAE: AB is common, AD = BE, and the included angles are equal, so by SAS they are congruent.

Step 3: Hence BD = AE, so (1/2)BC = (1/2)AC and BC = AC. The triangle is isosceles.

mcqs.q: The midpoint formula is:
mcqs.why: Review Exercise 16 identifies ((x1+x2)/2, (y1+y2)/2) as the midpoint formula: average the x values and average the y values separately.

mcqs.q: Midpoint of B(4,8) and A(2,6) is:
mcqs.why: Midpoint = ((4+2)/2, (8+6)/2) = (3,7). Each coordinate is the average of the two endpoint coordinates.

mcqs.q: Midpoint of P(-3,-1) and Q(5,2) is:
mcqs.why: Midpoint = ((-3+5)/2, (-1+2)/2) = (2/2, 1/2) = (1, 1/2). Note the y-average is one half, not a whole number.

mcqs.q: Midpoint of L(0,6) and M(-8,0) is:
mcqs.why: Midpoint = ((0-8)/2, (6+0)/2) = (-4, 3). The x-average is negative while the y-average stays positive.

mcqs.q: Centre of the circle with diameter endpoints A(-5,6) and B(3,-4) is:
mcqs.why: The centre is the midpoint of the diameter: ((-5+3)/2, (6-4)/2) = (-1, 1). Every diameter midpoint is the centre.

mcqs.q: Centre (3,4), one diameter endpoint (4,6): the other endpoint is:
mcqs.why: (4+x)/2 = 3 gives x = 2 and (6+y)/2 = 4 gives y = 2, so the other endpoint is (2,2), symmetric to (4,6) about the centre.

mcqs.q: Diameter endpoints A(-3,4) and B(11,6): the centre is:
mcqs.why: Centre = midpoint = ((-3+11)/2, (4+6)/2) = (8/2, 10/2) = (4,5). The radius is then half the diameter length.

mcqs.q: For those endpoints, the radius is:
mcqs.why: Diameter = sqrt(14^2 + 2^2) = sqrt(200) = 10sqrt(2), so radius = half of that = 5sqrt(2) units.

mcqs.q: Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other because:
mcqs.why: With O(0,0), A(a,0), C(b,d), B(a+b,d), both diagonals have midpoint ((a+b)/2, d/2). Same midpoint means they bisect each other.

mcqs.q: A triangle with two equal medians is:
mcqs.why: Equal medians AD and BE give congruent triangles ABD and BAE by SAS, so BD = AE and BC = AC. Hence the triangle is isosceles.
